speechtext: Hon. D. D. McKENZIE (Solicitor General) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 141, to repeal the Lake of the Woods Regulation Act, 1921.
Explain.

Some time in 1921,
before the opening of the session of that year, a certain agreement was arrived at between the Dominion of Canada, as represented by the right hon. the Prime Minister of that day, now leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and the province of Ontario, represented by the present Prime Minister of that province. I understand that the province of Manitoba also had something to do with the arrangement and was represented by its present Prime Minister. The agreement in question provided for the control of the Lake of the Woods and its water power by a board to be appointed jointly by the province of Ontario and the Dominion Government. To implement that agreement it was arranged that confirmatory legislation should be passed by this Parliament and by the legislation of Ontario. The then Prime Minister, the present right hon. leader of the Opposition, carried out his part of the arrangement and the act is known as Chapter 10 of the statutes of last year; but the Premier of Ontario was unable to carry a similar bill through the Ontario legislature. Upon his failure to do this he requested that no further steps should be taken until he was able to fulfil his part of the arrangement. However, as Chapter 10 was useless without joint legislation by Ontario, the right hon. gentleman introduced another bill under which the Dominion assumed absolute control of the Lake of the Woods, and this bill was passed by this Parliament and is now Chapter 38 of the statutes of last session. Section 10 of this act provides that if at any time the legislature of Ontario should enact the joint legislation agreed upon Chapter 38 should be repealed. The legislature of Ontario having recently passed the legislation contemplated in the agreement I have referred to. I am introducing this bill simply for the purpose of repealing Chapter 38.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Anent the explanation of the Solicitor General, I can only say that it affords a very good reason why there need be no such bill at all. He is quite right in stating that the second bill introduced last session contained a proviso that upon the government of Ontario implementing the agreement to which he refers, then the bill last introduced and passed here automatically is repealed, save as to one section which it is necessary to retain. If the act is repealed automatically when Mr. Drury carries out his promise, why does the Government introduce a special bill to effect the same purpose?
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of [DOT]the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 142, to amend the Indian Act.
He said: The first purpose of this bill is to repeal Section 7 dealing with the compulsory enfranchisement of Indians, which section was added to the act last session. I find that this feature meets with a great deal of opposition from the Indians themselves. Indeed, it is bitterly resented by the Six Nations Indians with whom we have had some little difficulty during the past month. This amendment simply repeals the section which gives the Deputy Superintendent General power to enfranchise an indian with or without his consent, and reverts to the former practice under which any indian desiring enfranchisement must make personal application.
The second section is intended to clarify the situation in regard to the ownership of land remaining in the control of the band, particularly land upon which returned indian soldiers have been re-established. I do not think there is really any legal doubt on the point, but inasmuch as an earlier amendment to the act has reference to the Soldiers' Settlement Act, which covers land taken as security by the Soldiers' Settlement Board, we are by this second section making it absolutely clear that the ownership of the land, whether occupied by a soldier settler or by any other indian, remains under the control of the band.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) :
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I read this morning a statement published in one of the local newspapers in connection with the action of the Pensions Board with reference to certain applications for pensions. I asked the chairman of the board to supply me with a memorandum regarding the matter; I hold it in my hand, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read it to the House. I may say that in the article referred to it was stated that this action of the Board of Pension Commissioners had relation to recent months. This is not a correct statement of the facts, as the House will see from the memorandum. The memorandum reads:
The minute made by the Board of Pension Commissioners under date of 29th September, 1921, was a statement in abbreviated form for the use of the board's medical advisors at headquarters.

The medical advisors in question were perfectly familiar with the points under discussion, and! the memorandum merely indicated and confirmed what had always been the interpretation of the policy of the board.
The board has always interpreted the intention of section 25 (3) of the act to mean that if an ex-member of the forces reached an actual theatre of war, and was found on discharge to have a physical condition which pre-existed enlistment, and which had progressed in any way on service, whether affected by service in any way or not-a simple progression having taken place on service-that although it were recognized that the condition must have preceded enlistment, and further recognized that in the ordinary course of events, in a sheltered existence, the condition would have progressed, no weight was to be given to such information, but the man would be pensionable, not only for the amount of progression, but for the total amount of the disability present.
Section 25 (3) of the act therefore would modify, to the extent outlined above, the qualifications for pension of any ex-member of the forces as defined by section (11) of the act. It was found, however, that there was a very occasional and rare case where a condition on discharge was found to exist and where it was established to the satisfaction of all concerned that there had been no progression of any kind on service; no cause or effect even remotely connected in any way with service; a condition present previous to enlistment, unchanged by, or on service. The further question then arose as to whether or not basically such a ease would be pensionable if there had been service in an actual theatre of war. The Board interpreted the act to mean that section 24 (3) in such a case would be modified by section fll) and that there must be a service connection in some way, shape or form, before there wou d be pension-ability.
The explanation of the Board in its Interpretation is very plain to the effect that if there has been any progression of a condition on service, if the condition is shown to be in any way worse on discharge than on admission, the pensioner, if he reached an actual theatre of war, must be considered, under Section 25 (3) of the act, to be pensionable for the whole extent of such disability. Section 2b (3) of the act states plainly that-"No deduction shall be made from the pension of any member of the
forces	on account of any disability
or disabling condition which existed In him previous to the time at which he became a member of the forces...." This has always been interpreted by the board to mean that before section 25 (3) of the act becomes applicable there must be presumed to be grounds for pension ; and section 25 (3) taken in conjunction with section (11) of the act, does not mean that an ex-member of the forces having served in an actual theatre of war must be pensioned for a disability, unless It can be shown that there has been an increase In the disabling condition on service.
It was pointed out to the board by Its medical advisors that those cases would be very rare where disability existed after service in an actual theatre of war, and where there would be, as a medical fact, no progression In the disabling condition. In this opinion, as advanced by its medical advisors, the board fully concurred.
An interpretation of the act which would permit of pensions being granted in cases where

Pensions Board
there was no claim on the part of any one that service had in any way affected the condition, or that there had been progression on service ; or, in other words, that the man entered the service and left it in exactly the same condition, would be to change entirely the principle upon which pensions are granted, and would be contrary to the statutes.
This is the memorandum which was handed to me by the Chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners. A memorandum setting forth the interpretation of the act was placed in the hands of the medical advisers of the board on the 29th of September, 1921, and' has not since been changed in any way.

speechtext: In connection with the statement which the minister has just made, there certainly does seem to be an impression-I have obtained it myself both through letters and statements in the press [DOT]-that certain changes have been made by the Board of Pension Commissioners making the regulations more strict. Is the minister in a position to make a statement in regard to that impression, which, judging from the number of letters I receive from soldiers in various parts of the country and from what I see in the press, seems to be pretty widespread.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am not in a position to make any statement in that regard. The board, I understand, considers a large number of cases every day which, of course, are never brought to the attention of the minister. I myself receive a number of- shall I say,-complaints from pensioners who claim that their pensions should not have been decreased or should have been increased, and in some cases that they should not have been cut off. In all such cases I have the file brought before me and go through it. Occasionally I discuss the case with the chairman of the board himself, and I may say that in most cases I have been able to give satisfaction to the complainant. The great majority of the cases which are submitted to the board never come before the minister. As the House is well aware, the Board of Pension Commissioners is a tribunal whose decisions are final.
Mr. MAN10N: I was not speaking of individual cases so much as of the general impression, which perhaps the minister himself has gained from the press, to the effect I stated. Rightly or wrongly many soldiers have the impression that the regulations or the rules regarding pensions have been made more strict. As the board is practically an independent body, and the minister the intermediary between the board and this House, would it not be possible for the board to have made the regulations more severe without the minister being aware of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If the board has interpreted the provisions in any narrower way recently, it has certainly not been in consequence of any instructions or suggestions that have been made by myself. I have never attempted to interfere with the work of the board. Occasionally I have asked the board to reopen and reconsider a case, with a view to using all their discretionary powers in favour of the applicant.

I did not mean to suggest that the minister had interfered in any way. I was just giving him the impression that I have received from a number of letters and from statements in the press. I might say that personally I have had a good deal of satisfaction in cases I have taken up with the board, particularly recently.

I should like to ask the minister whether his department has under consideration the advisability of amending that section of the act which sets a limitation on the time within which application for a pension may be considered. I have a case in my con-constituency of a young man who was killed overseas. During the time he was overseas his mother was receiving separation allowance and assigned pay, and she managed to save something from that, and for some three years she did not deem it necessary to make application for a pension. She was absolutely ignorant of the fact that the law provided a limitation. I believe the provision is that the application must be made within three years from the death of the person on whose account a pension is requested.

This whole discussion is out of order. The subject, I know, is a very important one, but I thought when the memorandum had been read by the minister the matter would rest there for

On motion of Hon. D. D. McKenzie (Solicitor General) Bill No. 132 to amend the Canada Temperance Act was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. 'Gordon in the Chair.
On Section 2-Upon receipt of an Order of Lieutenant-Governor in Council, the Governor in Council may issue proclamation.

I have just read over
this section and I assume that it is intended to apply to those provinces where export houses are at present maintained under Dominion license. I do not think there are any export houses or bonded warehouses in the province of Ontario, but there are such in some of the western provinces-I think in the province of Saskatchewan, and perhaps in the province of British Columbia, too. This section in its present form provides that on receipt of a certified copy of an Order in Council from the Lieutenant-Governor of a province the Government of Canada may pass an Order in Council fonbidding the further export from that province, or from Canada, of liquor now stored in bonded warehouses. I understand that in some of these bonded warehouses they have considerable stocks. If the section passes as it is now, confiscation of these stocks might result. I do not suppose it is the intention of the Government, or of the draughtsman of the bill, that liquor in any sense should be confiscated. What I would suggest is, that a reasonable time be given to the owners of liquor now in bonded warehouses for the disposal of their stocks-three months, or six months, or twelve months, whatever time the committee might think reasonable. I do not think it would be wise to pass the clause as it is now; it would be practically confiscation of property which is leg-

The real cause for the putting forward of this section, which came particularly from the province of Saskatchewan, is that a great deal of illegitimate selling and disposing of liquors is being done in some provinces because of the existence of warehouses where liquor is being kept. It has never been submitted to me, nor to any member of the Government that I am aware of, that any person in any province-at least, in the province of Saskatchewan-has any license for a bonded warehouse, or has a legally established warehouse, in which to keep liquor for the purpose of traffic. If there are such establishments, it has not been brought to my notice, except in a general way, such as the observations of the hon. member from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). If the hon. member, or any other hon. member, will satisfy this committee-he need not satisfy me more than anybody else-that the case which has been put forward is true, I would certainly not take any step that would confiscate any person's property. But, so far I am not aware, that neither the hon. member from South Wellington, or any other member of this House, has such definite information. However, the conditions in any province, with regard to this or any other matter, are better known to the members of the local government than to the members of the Government of Canada. This act cannot come into force in any province, it cannot have any effect, until the local government of the particular province in which it is asked for passes an Order in Council bringing it into force. If there is, in any province, a lawfully conducted business, and if the persons engaged in it have a right to carry it on, though it may be an unpopular business, if these people came before the government of that province, and said, You have the power under a Dominion statute to call in force in this province a law that will confiscate my property and cause me to lose a large amount of money; I am asking you not to put that law in force in this province until I have an opportunity of disposing of that property; if you do otherwise, you are doing a great wrong, and forfeiting a great deal of that property ",-it strikes me the premier, and government of that province, would

very properly say, "Very good, we shall not do anything that will affect your property until you have an opportunity of disposing of it, providing you have it legally in stock Now, if there is to be leniency of that kind shown, it is just as much the power of one government as of the other. All this parliament is doing is passing a law, and making it optional for any province to put it in force. That kind of legislation in regard to liquor has been gaining ground for the last ten years. Practically, nothing has been done in this House in regard to intoxicating liquor for a number of years anyhow unless it is first approved by the province. All we have done is to say " You can

Where do they get the power to do it, if it is done legally?

I am satisfied that for the last year and a half no person, either in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, or Saskatchewan or Alberta, could import any intoxicating liquor legally, nor could they manufacture it legally. That provision is to be found in part IV. of the Canada Temperance Act. If I am asked to-day in this House by what right are you going to put a proviso in the act to protect people in Alberta or Saskatchewan who have those houses in which they hold liquor for import?-by what law do they get it in, or by what law are they holding it?-I cannot give any answer. If there is any hon. member who knows there is such a law, and who knows it is legitimate property and legitimate trade, he has the right, the power, and the privilege of presenting that authority to the House. I am unfortunate enough not to know there is any such law, and I am unfortunate enough not to know that there is, in that province, such legal business, recognized in Saskatchewan, and until it is brought home to me that legal business is affected, I do not feel called

upon to ask this i'cii iiuu*ctiL Oi to legalize, to protect, or safeguard, any business, however popular it might be under certain circumstances, carried on in this country. If anybody in the House will move such an amendment, I will certainly as representing the Government, not accept it. Explaining the liquor business in Saskatchewan seems to be as difficult as explaining the wheat board. I may say that a situation grew up in Saskatchewan* as a result of the interim of four months between the vote taken on the referendum in November, 1920, and the enacting of the law. During that time a large number of export warehouses were established in Saskatchewan, containing from one to ten carloads of liquor. There was nothing illegal about it. They took advantage of the long period between the time the will of the people was expressed at the poll and the putting of the law into force. I do not know how many millions worth of property was stowed away during those four months. I know there were 59 export liquor houses-not bonded warehouses; the hon. member from South Wellington is mistaken in regard to that. None of these houses is either licensed or bonded; they are quite distinct from bonded warehouses; they are there, and the province cannot get rid of them. In 1917 the province of Saskatchewan passed an Act-and so did the province of Alberta-attempting to get rid of the export houses, and failed, because the Act was declared by the court to be ultra vires. The desire out there, no matter how foolish it may appear down here, is to get rid of the liquor in that province. We want to be dry, and we have not been dry largely because of the existence of these export houses. In order to carry out the will of the people, in so far as provincial law is ineffectual for the purpose, it is proposed1 to pass this supplementary legislation. The whole question is, how long shall we give these export houses to get rid of their wares? It is true that they got these supplies in legally in the first instance, but they have no real right to keep them in the province now. Now, 1 am not an authority on the question as to how long it takes to drink a million dollars' worth of liquor, which I understand

Canada Temperance Act
is the estimated quantity in Saskatchewan. There was several million dollars' worth there, but it has all been consumed, presumably outside the province.
Are they not complaining about the dry season in Saskatchewan?

Yes, but that is a different sort of dryness. Let me say that this is no joking matter in Saskatchewan, or in Alberta either. Like the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie), I have no desire whatever, and I do not think anybody has, to confiscate the property of any one whether it be liquor or anything else. We want to be fair to these men. They put one over on the province in getting the liquor in in the first place, although the law did not forbid them to do so; and I have no doubt that they reaped a substantial harvest thereby. Well, if they should happen to lose a little they must take the chance. Mind you, I do not take the ground that I want them to lose anything; I simply want them to get out, and that is why I desire to see the legislation go through. If it appeals to the committee, as I think it will, as a fair proposition that the will of the people out there be given expression to, then there should be no trouble about the matter. We do the same thing in the case of British Columbia or any other wet province. British Columbia wants to handle wet goods and we are facilitating the people there in carrying out their wishes. But in Saskatchewan and Alberta-at least I can speak for my own province-the people want the place to be dry and they feel that their wish in this regard cannot be carried out so long as these export houses remain there. I have suggested that these houses should be given three months to get rid of their liquor. As I say, they are presumably not doing an illegal business; they got the liquor in legally, and are shipping it out legally. But liquor leaks out, and it is impossible to observe the will of the people with these institutions carrying on business in this way. I have suggested three months to my colleague, but he apparently does not favour that suggestion at all, because he feels that these houses are there illegally. At any rate, that is how I interpret his attitude. My hon. friend to my right, on the other hand, thinks that they are there legally, and I am disposed to agree with him. And we cannot get rid of them because of our provincial
limitations; only this Parliament can put them out. If a longer period than three months is requested in which to dispose of the liquor without risk of loss, then I take the ground that the law should be changed with regard to the time limit between votes. So far as I can recall- I have not had time to look into the law, but I think I am right-when we voted on the matter in November, 1920, we did so on the understanding that another vote could not be taken for three years; in other words, the will of the people could not be consulted again until the law had been given a fair trial. The intent of legislative bodies when they put a law on the statute book is that it shall be given a fair trial. That period of three years between votes was regarded as a fair term. One year and four months has passed of that period, but the law has not had what can be regarded as a fair trial simply because of the existence of these export houses and, as a matter of fact, the dry sentiment of this province has been prejudicially affected by the operation of this business. If you allow these houses eight months, say, in which to get rid of their liquor, it will 'be eight months added to the year and four months that has passed in which the law has had but a partial and unsatisfactory trial, that is to say, two years of the three, which was the period of trial, will have passed without affording anything like a proper test. I might put it this way: whatever time we allow these houses to get rid of their liquor will be added to the wet era, and correspondingly subtracted from the period of trial. My proposal is that if you extend the three months I have suggested to six months you should correspondingly extend the period between votes. As a matter of fact, there is no real prohibition in these provinces at all. The present condition is perhaps in some respects worse than legalized traffic. I am not by any means suggesting that there should be legalized traffic, but I say that the present state of things in some respects is worse than that, because there are a great many objectionable features in connection with it. I repeat, we do not want to confiscate property or do anything that is not fair, but we do want to carry out the people's wishes. The law applies to the other provinces as well, and whenever they so desire they can take advantage of it. The province of Saskatchewan has already sent down to my colleague two strongly worded
Canada Temperance Act

petitions from the legislature during the past couple of sessions asking that the present condition in Saskatchewan be terminated. They have expressed themselves in a pronounced way on the matter.

The question before the committee is, shall we confiscate certain property which is now in Saskatchewan, or shall we not? I understand that the question has particular reference to that province. The Solicitor-General (Mr. McKenzie) declares that he is not in favour of making any amendment to this section, while the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who comes from that province and probably knows something about the benefits of a little liquor there, suggests a period of three months in which the people who have this property stored in their warehouses shall get rid of it. The Solicitor-General has told us that this liquor is illegally in the province of Saskatchewan. I rather fancy that he did not look into the legal aspect of the case with the same care which he usually exercises when drafting bills that present -some legal difficulties. This liquor is legally in the province of Saskatchewan; it came there legally. If it is not there legally, then, of course, the authorities should forthwith confiscate it. How is it that the Department of Customs has not confiscated these goods if they are illegally in Saskatchewan? They are there legally, and all that is asked now is that a reasonable time be given these people to get their goods out of the province. They are engaged in a traffic which, although it may be unpopular, is none the less legal. It must be borne in mind that the sale of spirituous liquor in the western hemisphere is somewhat restricted at present, in fact there is practically no market for it. A small quantity of these goods might possibly be sold in Mexico or the West Indies, but a million dollars' worth -and I am told that is the quantity they have there-cannot be -sold in Europe, which is about the only market left, within a period of three months, for it takes a considerable time to dispose of such a large quantity. Therefore these people ask-and I think it is a reasonable request-that they should have a sufficient period of time within which to dispose of their property. I think that under the circumstances six months is not an unreasonable time to be given for the disposal of goods which cannot be offered for sale on the local market. If you fix a shorter [ Mr. Motherwell. ]
time, say three months, it is practically equivalent to confiscation, and I am sure it is not the desire of this Parliament to take such harsh measures. In view of all the circumstances I am in favour of giving these people a reasonable time within which to dispose of their property, and therefore I beg leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell):
That at the end of section 157 there be added the following proviso: "Providing that such order-in-council shall n-ot be passed prior to the 1st day of January, 1923 ''
You say that this business is now carried on legally. What is the practice followed? What licenses are granted and what are the restrictions on export business?

I am not familiar with
the law of Saskatchewan, but the business would be legal even if the goods were merely kept in warehouses, and I fancy, that before this law comes into force the goods can be legally exported from the province. This section declares that " on and after the Lieutenant Governor in Council notifies the Secretary of State, the goods cannot be exported." Consequently there is nothing for these owners to do but to destroy their property, and it is for the purpose of enabling them to get it out of the province before prohibition against exportation is put into effect that I am moving this amendment.
Mr. LEW'IS: I concur in the judgment of the Solicitor General. I think that the people of Saskatchewan themselves have the right to say whether there shall be an extended time of three months or otherwise, for they are in a better position to know what time is required to get rid of these liquors than hon. members down here. For that reason I am not in favour of the amendment. We are sufficiently familiar with the men who control the liquor stores in Saskatchewan to suspect that these liquors did not come into the province in a very legitimate manner. It did not take them very long to bring in their goods when they knew that Saskatchewan was against importation; and it does seem to me that when Saskatchewan has voted definitely against the sale of liquor within the province, it cannot be said that these liquors are there legitimately ; they1 were forced upon the province against the expressed will of the electorate. Therefore, I think the bill should

be passed without any amendment whatever. The government of Saskatchewan know the local conditions thoroughly, and they also know the men who own these liquor stores, and if the members of that government feel it is essential to grant the owners a three months' extension of time to get rid of their property, well and good, but in view of the expressed will of the people of the province the quicker we get rid of this menace the better. We in Saskatchewan do not believe that it is a legitimate business, we do not believe that those who engage in it have a right to bring their goods into the province against the expressed will of the people. For that reason I am heartily in favour of the bill being passed without amendment, leaving it to the provincial authorities who know the whole situation to grant any extension of time that may be necessary to enable the owners to get rid of this stuff that is destroying the moral fibre of our life.

I think this committee is wasting a lot of sympathy on the men who are engaged in this export liquor business. I am confident that if hon. members had an opportunity of becoming acquainted with the methods pursued by these liquor exporters they would not spend five minutes sympathizing with them. As the Minister of Agriculture has said, these people took advantage of the opportunity they had before the new law came into force to stock up. They are not exporting to Europe now, as has been suggested, but they are supplying bootleggers in the province and conveying the liquor across the international boundary line into the United States Now', every bottle of liquor carried across the line is carried across in defiance of the law. Recently I took a clipping from an American newspaper severely criticizing the Canadian Government for allowing the traffic to go on. I have not the clipping at hand, in fact I lent it to the Prime Minister to peruse. This is the way the business is carried on. Fast motor cars are loaded with liquor in the middle of the night, and the men engaged in this business make for the international boundary line, followed perhaps by a police automobile. The men in both cars are well armed, and in many cases a fight takes place on the road. Now, the people in the southern part of the province when they are out driving do not enjoy the prospect of being shot in the course of one of these running fights.
Canada Temperance Act
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of having these goods confiscated and destroyed by the government of Saskatchewan?

I am coming to that in a minute. The men who carry liquor to the United States in this way have boasted again and again that in one trip they make enough money to buy an expensive automobile such as a McLaughlin. Now, if they have been making that profit for about two years, I do not think we need worry very much about whether this liquor is confiscated or not. Those men do not want time to sell their goods in Europe. If they knew that in three months' time the law was going to be changed, they would get rid of this liquor very quickly. They have plenty of associates in the business, and with few exceptions they are a bad bunch. I have no hesitation in making that statement; it can be backed up by the men who live in the southern part of the province. I have been down there and have been told by the people: "This is the road on which the bootleggers carry on their traffic during the night; they pass our very doors." The business is carried on by the use of the fastest automobiles that can be got. A short time ago an automobile started from one of these export liquor houses and some twelve miles out the police stopped them and took charge of the liquor; yet under the law nothing could be done. I would like to read to you an extract from some remarks made by Chief Justice Brown when one of these cases was tried before him. I suggest that those hon. members who have sympathy for this people should listen to this:
We have our own province in which there exists a prohibitory law and likewise we see liquor imported from our own province into neighbouring provinces, and we sit down practically helpless, doing nothing and apparently not wanting to do anything to help them enforce that law. The matter it seems to me could be largely remedied by a simple piece of legislation on the part of the Parliament of Canada, making it illegal to export liquor or sell liquor for export to any country or any province where prohibition is in force. As I have already indicated I cannot believe that the people of Canada generally realize the demoralizing condition of affairs that exists; otherwise, it seems to me the Parliament of Canada would have before this passed legislation to the effect I have already suggested. We can only hope that the matter of our responsibility in this matter and the true condition of affairs may be more fully realized by our people generally and if_ it is, then it seems to me we will get the legislation that is necessary to remedy the situation. Not only has this court been largely oocupied
Canada Temperance Act

with cases that have arisen as a result of this traffic, but the same has characterized all the courts that have been held in the southern part of this province during the last few years. It is a condition of affairs that certainly should not exist, and it seems to me fit and proper that I should call attention to the matter in this way at this particular time.
This is not a matter of prohibition or otherwise; it is a case of complying with the expressed wish of the province to be freed from this traffic. I can scarcely conceive of the people of Canada wishing to continue to force this sort of thing on the province of Saskatchewan when the people there have expressed themselves as they have. I entirely concur in the view of the Solicitor General: the people of Saskatchewan know the conditions even better than we in this House do; they know just about how much consideration should, be extended to those affected by any change and I cannot conceive of their doing any injustice in that connection. In fact, they can say how long a time the persons affected shall have within which to dispose of his liquor. Personally I think six months is too long; I think the Solicitor General's view is the correct one.

This legislation seems to be proceeding upon proper lines. In fact, it conforms to the policy of the late government, which was to give effect to the wishes of the different communities which had adopted laws dealing with this liquor question. We always held ourselves as desirous of implementing the legislation on the one hand and the desires on the other of the provincial governments. So far as this particular matter is concerned, if my recollection is correct the position taken by the Customs Department under the former government-and still maintained, I believe, under the present Administration-is that no bonded warehouse licences should be issued in any of the provinces except with the consent of the local administration. It seems to me that, carrying out the policy of implementing provincial legislation and the provincial desire wherever possible, it is the duty of this House to take the action proposed on this occasion. Now, we have to bear in mind the distinction between a business which may be inherently vicious and one which may simply have developed into the practice of rum-running, and the like. If the whole of this business is illegal; if the storing of liquor in these warehouses is against the law, why is section 163 drafted as it is in the bill? That is the section which is the prohibitory provision. It says: 
Subject to the provisions of subsection two of this section, and notwithstanding the provisions of this or any other act to the contrary, no person shall Import, send, take or transport into any province in which the prohibitions of this subsection are in force any intoxicating liquor.
But I find an exception, as follows:
The importation of intoxicating liquor into a province by a person engaged in and carrying on the business of exporting intoxicating liquor from that province, where the intoxicating liquor so imported is imported solely for the purpose of his export business and while kept by him in the province, is kept in a liquor warehouse which conforms in all respects to the requirements of the law governing such warehouses, and when sold or disposed of by him is actually exported from that province:

I may point out that the first part of this bill is an amendment of Part IV of the Canada Temperance Act, passed in 1919. The section to which my hon. friend refers may be regarded as new legislation; it has no connection with the section we are considering. It is an amendment of Part V.
Then my hon. friend is now legalizing, under Part V, that business which he had previously looked upon as illegal.
Part V has reference to provinces which have themselves undertaken the whole of the business of handling the liquor, as in the case of British Columbia and Quebec.

I am inclined to agree with the ex-Minister of Finance that in any part of the Dominion where there is a desire to get rid of the liquor business, it should be within, entirely within, the jurisdiction of the province or section, as the case may be, to deal with the matter. Under the old Canada Temperance Act, as I understood it, any province or county could, by a vote, put that act into force. Under the old act, however, importation was allowed into all the provinces, notwithstanding the fact that the Canada Temperance Act was in force. I know that in the city of Quebec the Canada Temperance Act was in force, and in the rest of the province, with two exceptions, we had the Quebec Prohibition Act, under the provisions of which there could be no importation into any part of the province. But it was held that there could be importation into the city of Quebec under the provisions of the Canada Temperance Act. Subsequently the Doherty Act was passed, which was an endeavour to extend to the provinces the right to prohibit importation. But it was

Canada Temperance Act
found, I believe, that it did not go that far -and, so far as that is concerned, the act was held to be unconstitutional. If I understand this legislation correctly, it is an endeavour to go a step further and to give to the provinces exactly what they want. 1 am entirely in accord with that. But under the provisions of the act as it has existed these people who do have stocks on hand had them there legally, and it is for this House to decide whether, if citizens holding stock there legally, no matter what they may have been doing with them heretofore-and the stocks held have been stated to be worth a million dollars-we should legislate here to-day and say that ipso facto on the passing of the Order in Council, all that merchandise shall be destroyed without warning. This is a question that has often been debated; it has been debated in England and almost every other country in the world, and I do not think a case can be found where the government of a country confiscated the goods of its citizens without giving them some time to dispose of the stocks on hand. If I have a suggestion to make to the mover, it would be that the government of Saskatchewan be authorized to pass their Order in Council at once, and that once the Order in Council is passed these people be given time-the six months that is spoken of-to ship their goods out. The goods will then remain in bond under the control of the government, and they cannot be bootlegged throughout the province, whereas if you leave these stocks there and give them this six months without passing the Order in Council, there will be a danger of spreading the stocks throughout the province in the meantime. If you allow the province to pass their Order in Council immediately, and give these people six months to dispose of their goods before confiscating, that would seem to me to be much more fair, and in accord with precedent in every country that I ever heard of.

Just one further thought arising out of what my hon. friend has said: I do not think any one of us wants to do anything we ought not to do. I think we are all anxious to see that the wishes expressed by the province of Saskatchewan be carried out. Why cannot this act be passed just as it is without doing the slightest degree of harm? In the first instance, the local government have to act. They have a right to pass their Order in Council and to fix their day. In the second instance, their act by itself is
nothing, as I read this section, until this Government gives effect to that Order in Council.

If I may interrupt
the hon. gentleman, I do not think he has quite understood the section. If we pass the act as it is, the local government would have absolutely no power to give the delay to which he refers. Otherwise, I would not have a word to say. But neither the local government, nor this Government without the necessary authority, could give one minute's delay.

I would point out that this is the usual section, clothed in the ordinary language, giving jurisdiction to a government to act by Order in Council. We know the difficulties which always attend the administration of government, and I venture to say that if this act goes through just as it is, it will be some little time before it is put into final effect. The section reads:
Upon receipt by the Secretary of State of Canada of a duly certified copy of an order in council passed by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province in which the importation of intoxicating liquors into the province has been prohibited under this part, and in which such prohibition is still in force, requesting that the keeping of intoxicating liquor in such province for export and the exportation of intoxicating liquor therefrom by persons other than brewers and distillers duly licensed by the Government of Canada, be forbidden-
Forbidden as and from when? Surely there is an effective date to be given in that Order in Council, and after that first Order in Council is passed, it is not effective unti the Governor in Council by Order in Council declares-it says "may", not "shall"- that such prohibition shall come into force in such province on a day to be named in such order. It does not seem to me that the respective governments will know very much more, with the whole facts of the case before them, than this House can.

I thoroughly agree with
the sentiments that have been expressed by many hon. members who have spoken. I do think the province should have the say as to the time when these provisions are to come into effect. I would recommend to the minister that the wording be changed slightly to read something as follows:
-requesting that the keeping o'f intoxicating liquor in such province for export and the exportation of intoxicating liquor therefrom by persons other than brewers and distillers duly licensed by the Government of Canada be forbidden on and after a date to be named, and

the Governor in Council may by Order in Council declare that such prohibition shall come into force in such province on the day fixed by the Order in Council of the executive of the provincial government.
The word "order" in that section surely refers to the federal order rather than to the provincial. Whenever a term like that is used, it always refers to the one nearest it.

That is the difficulty that
I see.

One of them is
the Governor in Council, and the other is the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.

That is quite right, as I
understand it. The word "order" last mentioned in the paragraph refers to the order of the Governor in Council, not of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
That is right.

My suggestion is that the Lieutenant-Governor in Council not only ask that the exportation he forbidden, but also ask that it be forbidden as of a particular date, and that that date be adopted by the Governor in Council in the Order in Council which they propose. It may be that that is the intention of this act but on a casual reading I would say that it is not. It does seem to me that the provincial government should be the best judge as to when the Order in Council shall become effective.
There has been some misapprehension, I think, in connection with the operation of this particular amendment. The press have, to some extent, at least, circulated the idea that it is applicable only to the province of Saskatchewan. I may say that that has caused some concern in the province of Alberta, for I have received a telegram from the Attorney General of that province in which he requests that similar legislation be passed for the province of Alberta. He also points out in his telegram :
The Alberta cabinet meeting to-day-
That is yesterday.

strongly urge this legislation be applied to the province of Alberta, as our greatest difficulty under Liquor Act results from the operation of liquor export houses.
Now we are anxious to give the province the fullest possible control in order that the existing laws may be made watertight, and may be effectively enforced. The greatest difficulty in the way of doing that

has been tne operations of these liquor exporting houses. I have only been able to consider casually the purposes of the bill, and I would like to receive an assurance from the Solicitor General that it contains nothing that would limit its operation to the province of Saskatchewan.
It applies to all the provinces.
I wanted an assurance from the Solicitor General that it applies also to the province of Alberta, if other provinces are going to get the benefit of it.
That is the way I understand it.

I want to express my approval of the bill, especially since we have been assured it covers all the provinces of the Dominion. The province of Ontario has gone to its limit in regard to temperance legislation; if not, it is endeavouring to do so. Any federal law which would strengthen its hands and enable it to fully carry out and enforce the provisions of the Ontario Temperance Act will be heartily received throughout the province. We are all aware of the bootlegging and the disorderly conduct which has occurred in western Ontario in the past, and especially the transportation of liquor from that part of this country to the United States. Any legislation prohibiting the transportation of liquor other than by steam railway or water will undoubtedly strengthen the hands of Ontario in its endeavours to put an end to that traffic. It will stop the carriage of liquors by motor vehicles along the public highways of the province, and will be of the utmost importance in strengthening the hands of the provincial authorities in their endeavours to carry out the provincial legislation to the fullest extent.

It is quite evident that the bill is intended in its application to prohibition provinces to increase the power of the local authorities so as to give effect to prohibitive legislation; and in provinces where the provincial governments are dealing in liquor to give them a further monopoly of the liquor business. Now it has been stated in the province of British Columbia, for instance by the Attorney General of the province, that the provincial authorities were unable to administer the local liquor law satisfactorily because of the operations of export houses, and that until he gets co-operation in the way of federal legislation he cannot im-

Canada Temperance Act
prove his administration of the provincial liquor law. I would ask the Solicitor General if the views and requests of the Attorney General of British Columbia have been fully met in the present bill?

When this bill was first drafted its general nature and applications had reference to British Columbia because the request for federal legislation came from there. The bill was drafted by the Attorney General of British Columbia with some assistance, I think, from the Department of Justice; I have every reason to believe that as it stands to-day it grants all that was asked for by the province of British Columbia through its Attorney General.

My constituency is in the southern part of Saskatchewan and there are several export houses established there, one of them being located in a horse livery barn only about twenty-five miles from the international boundary line. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, an export house keeping its liquor in a horse livery barn! Four, five or half a dozen high-powered cars are used for the carriage of liquor across the boundary line, and these cars travel at the rate of about forty or fifty miles an hour on their nefarious mission. I consider these operations are a disgrace to any Canadian province. People in Saskatchewan have protested against such proceedings, and have expressed their wishes to see them abolished, but we find that the liquor interests are strong fighters; they have put up a fight worthy of a better cause, and when we nail them on one point they have recourse to some other. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) says it is not fair, in a sense, to close these liquor houses out in three months. I contend that the liquor interests have established these export houses to frustrate the laws of Saskatchewan, and they break not only the Canadian law but the law of the country to the south of us. While I do not want to be harsh or unreasonable in this matter, yet I think that men who have been deliberately and persistently frustrating the law cannot now claim very much leniency. In the past they have taken advantage of the leniency of the law right along. We do not want to confiscate their property, but we do want to place the responsibility for this traffic where it belongs. The provincial authorities have been saying that they have gone to the limit and have done
all they could, and that it is now up to the federal authorities to act. In Saskatchewan we want to see this bill go through as it stands so that the wishes of the province with respect to prohibition of the liquor traffic may be carried out.

When this bill was originally drafted it was prepared by the authorities for the province of British Columbia and the province of Quebec, and was not intended at all to apply to any of the provinces that have voted dry. It was only after the bill was introduced, or after it began to be studied by the officers of the Crown, that its provisions were extended to the dry provinces. Unfortunately I have seconded the motion of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), but I am a little sorry for it now because he is asking that six months be allowed before the province should put this law into force. Now, I consulted with the Attorney General of Quebec, and discussed this matter with him. That province wants to get authority to control the transportation just as the province of Saskatchewan wishes to do, but I believe-although the Attorney General has not so informed me-that if he were consulted as regards giving the proprietors time, to dispose of the stocks which they now legally hold, he would be willing to give them six months. At any rate, it is desired that the legislation come into effect at once so that control may be vested in the provincial government within two weeks or a month from the time the law goes into force. I would therefore suggest to the Solicitor General that the committee report progress and see if it is not possible to redraft this amendment in order to bring the act into force, with the understanding that the provincial governments be empowered to give these proprietors six months' notice.

I quite
agree with what has been said, that the whole trend of federal prohibitive legislation has been in the direction of placing the responsibility for enacting and enforcing prohibitory laws on the provinces. That is quite as it should be. The present bill proceeds along the same lines by supplementing acts that have been passed by the provincial legislatures. Although the traffic in Saskatchewan which has been discussed this afternoon is legal, it is quite obvious that it has been carried
Canada Temperance Act

on contrary to the very emphatically expressed opinion of the people. If parties imported into Saskatchewan a few million dollars' worth of liquor between the time the people expressed their opinion, and the time the law went into effect, if they did not see fit to secure licenses from the federal authorities to conduct a bonded warehouse, I do not think this Parliament should regard them in any other light than as outlaws. They simply carried on this business, taking advantage of a loophole in the law, and have no right to expect the protection of Parliament. I think the provinces should have the absolute right to determine when this supplementing legislation shall go into effect. Although I am not a lawyer, I am a little doubtful whether this section, as it stands, gives them that right. I think, as pointed out by an hon. member, a little change in that wording is necessary. As I view it, this legislation is going to give the province the right to pass an Order in Council, and when that is done, the Dominion authority shall pass an Order in Council, naming the day on which the provincial Order in Council shall go into effect.

That is not quite the procedure. The Lieutenant Governor's order in council has nothing to do with the question of the date when the law shall go into effect. He simply makes the request that this Government shall bring the law into effect; and this is following exactly the provisions of part IV of the Canada Temperance Act. I am quite familiar with the steps to be taken under Part IV of the Canada Temperance Act. That law was passed by this Parliament in 1919, and it contained a proviso that, if any province asked that this law should go into force within its bounds, the legislature of the province would pass a resolution asking the Government of Canada for an election, so that the people of the province could declare their will as to whether such a law should be enacted. When the Government received that resolution they called an election. The election would be held and then, by Order in Council, the Dominion government would bring the law into force. The province never had anything to say as to when the law should come into force, they were simply making the request, and every step in regard to it was taken by the Dominion government, except that the request for it, and the request for the preliminaries, came from the recognized authorities under the law. In draughting and providing for this bill, amending Part IV of the Canada Tem-

perance Act, we are simply following the statute.
Would it not be quite proper to give to the provinces the privilege of requesting that this section should come into effect upon a certain date?

My hon. friend is an honest and well-meaning man, but, as he says he is not a lawyer. If he were a lawyer he would understand that we cannot delegate any power to the local legislature.
They have powers given to them
5 p.m. under the British North America Act which are exclusively theirs, and we cannot give them any of our powers-these powers we have to exercise ourselves. We cannot say to any province, "you shall on a certain date bring a certain act into force." They are absolute monarchs of all they survey within their own jurisdiction.

I am entirely in sympathy with the proposed bill, but, as I understand the discussion, the date when exportation from the various provinces shall cease depends entirely upon the federal government, and the proposal in the amendment, I believe, is that the date shall be extended until the first of January. I am very much opposed to that, for this reason: there are two export houses in the constituency which I represent. I was in that district last fall, and I will say, in all frankness, that the situation there is a discredit to the authority which allows it to go on. There would appear- to be, in the province of Saskatchewan, some large stores of liquor, because almost every week, at the little town of Govenlock, in my constituency, liquor is unloaded by the carload. I do not think that anything is gained by extending the time for six months. I would not wish that the date should be set at, probably, less than three months. There must be in Saskatchewan somewhere large stores of liquor.
Amendment (Mr. Jacobs) negatived.
We have voted down the suggestion that the time limit be six months. As it stands now, it might be six years or it might be sixty years.
You have no faith in yourselves?

The time for bringing prohibition into force is plainly in the

Canada Temperance Act
hands of the Governor General in Council, and, I think, my hon. friends can quite well leave it to them.
I have suggested that the section stand until we understand what it means.

I do not see what there is in this section that requires to stand. It is perfectly clear to every one. The amendment was voted down, and what is it that is going to stand? Is it a case of Micawber, waiting for something to turn up?

I think we should get some assurance from the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) that he is really in earnest and really honest about it. The Minister of Agriculture is suspicious of the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie), and has no faith in him. He does not like to trust the act to him and other members of the Government. We may be getting a little sidelight as to why some great reforms promised during the last election have not been carried out. Perhaps, it is not because a certain minister was a private citizen at the time. It may be because he finds some wicked colleague will not allow him to carry his design into execution. The only thing this matter need stand for is the possibility of a reconciliation amongst the members of the Government, and the establishment of the mutual confidence that should exist.

The Governor in Council would then know exactly when the province desired to have the act put into force. In order to ascertain the views of the committee I would move that after the word " forbidden," in the twenty-second line, the words " on a date therein named " be inserted, and that the last two lines be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

I appeal to the committee for some consideration in this matter. I stated a little while ago that the bill was drafted partly by the Attorney-General of British Columbia, partly by the Attorney General of Quebec, and partly by some legal authorities in Saskatchewan; and with any assistance that I could secure, there fell to me the very hard task of so adjusting and welding together these different fragments as to produce the bill in its present form. I have put days and nights into the1 work, and have devoted to it all the energies I possess, and I do dislike to have it broken up. It is all right as it is, and should not be changed.

I have listened to the member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), and although there seems to be some point to his amendment, I think the power is already m the provinces. The section reads:
Upon receipt by the Secretary of State of Canada of a duly certified copy of an Order In Council passed iby ithe Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province, etc.

Canada Temperance Act
The Lieutenant Governor need not take action until he- is satisfied that the time is ripe for it. He need not apply to the federal government until the province is ready to have the act put into force.

I am heartily in accord with the remarks of the Solicitor General. It does not require one line of legislation to enable the province to make a request, and even if there were some supererogation in the draughtsmanship of the bill conferring power in the matter, that power already exists. A province can come and ask for anything; it need not be empowered to do that. It would not vitiate the Order in Council contemplated if it did state a date and request that on that date the federal government should bring its legislation into effect; it would not hurt a bit. But from a very short experience of the work of government, I may suggest that it would be quite easy for a province, perhaps very zealou-s and1 well-intentioned, to name a date that would not possibly permit the consideration of their request in time to issue the proclamation to bring the law into force on that date. It is not possible to drop all other business of the Dominion and take up an isolated subject like this. The province might fix, for instance, one week from the date of the passing of legislation. I am not prepared to concur in the proposal that the province should fix the date. I am certainly not here in support of the present Government, but I am not here to raise fantastic objections to their mode of carrying on business, and I should have to assume that they intended, in a sense, to betray the province which made a request of this kind if I agreed to the proposal that the province should fix the date. I believe that when a province makes the request, the Order in Council will be granted just so soon as it can be passed in the ordinary course of business. I am not going to accuse the Government of intended bad faith, when I have not the slightest bit of evidence o<n which to base such an accusation. It will be quite time enough to deal with the Government when it is found acting in bad faith. I do not anticipate that that opportunity will ever occur in this matter, I am quite prepared to trust the Solicitor General and' his confreres, in the perfect assurance that the request of any province will be met in proper time without the slightest attempt to do anything other than exactly what the province asks.

The implicit trust of the member for St. John in the Government to-day is very amazing, and it does suggest the "morganatic alliance" of which we have heard before. I have also every confidence in the Government in this matter, but my intention was simply to give the provincial government an opportunity to convey to this Government their desire that the prohibition should come into force on a particular date. I am satisfied that the Governor in Council will see to it that the request of any province, regardless of its politics, will receive proper consideration. If the Solicitor General feels that he cannot accept this very simple amendment I am not going to press it.

Subsection (h) of
Section 158 provides:
The carriage or transportation through such province of intoxicating Mquoi which may lawfully be exported therefrom shall only be by means of a common carrier by water or by railway and not otherwise,
It is pointed out to me that the prohibition might go so far as not to allow delivery from a brewery, distillery or warehouse, as the case may be, to the common carrier by water or by railway, when the brewery, distillery or warehouse was not situated on a railway siding. I would therefore suggest to the Solicitor General that after the word "otherwise" in the fourth line he add the words, "excepting for delivery to and from such common carrier." Without that amendment a brewer delivering to a train or steamboat might have his motor truck seized and confiscated.

In the event of this
amendment being accepted, would there be anything to prevent those delivering liquor from travelling to any part of the province so long as later on they were going to deliver to a common carrier?

The delivery must be from the warehouse to the common carrier, and I presume if those delivering are found several miles away from the point of delivery they would be presumed to be going somewhere else with the liquor.

The word "direct"
would cover that point.

While the amendment offered at first glance looks very innocent, we who have seen the facility with which such provisions of the law can be violated are a little suspicious

Canada Shipping Act
of its effect-not of the intention of the hon. member. For instance, on the prairies the points of delivery are frequently very many miles apart, and I know of one particular road between two towns some forty-two or forty-three miles apart which was kept open last winter for weeks after the ordinary automobile traffic ceased in order that this particular traffic might continue.
This will apply only to British Columbia and Quebec, because you will not have any export houses in Saskatchewan after this law comes into effect.
If that is correct the hon. gentleman's amendment may be accepted. But we have warehouses there even if they are not used for export.

I agree with the hon. gentleman for I had charge for several years of the enforcement of the prohibition law in Quebec, and I know all the difficulties he speaks of. But this was pointed out to me as a defect which should be remedied.
Inasmuch as the Solicitor General thinks his bill should not be spoiled seeing he spent so much time on it, and as I am a supporter of the Government, I shall oppose the amendment.
I object to the words, "to and from the common carriers". That is to say, between common carriers themselves liquor can be transported, if I understand the amendment aright.
No.
Why not strike out the words, "and from"?

That would not do. Supposing you take shipments from the province of Ontario, where most of the distilleries are, and bring them into the province of Quebec, you land them at the Bonaven-ture station, Montreal, and have to take them to the government warehouse.
Quite right.
