House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend sections 850 and 854 of Part XII of the Canada Shipping Act, chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, relating to Public Harbours and Harbour Masters, and to provide:-
1.	That section 850 be amended so as to provide that Part XII shall apply to such ports only as have been or may be hereafter designated for that purpose by proclamation, or have been or may be created public harbours by proclamation under that Part, but shall not apply to the ports of Quebec, Montreal and Three Rivers in the province of Quebec, to the ports of Toronto, Hamilton and Belleville in the province of Ontario, to the iport of Halifax in the province of Nova Scotia, to the port of iSt. John in the province of New Brunswick, to the ports of Vancouver, North Fraser and New Westminster in the province of British Columbia, or to the port of Winnipeg and St. Boniface in the province of Manitoba, or to ary harbour or port with respect ito which there is or may be established under an act of the Parliament of Canada a harbour commission or other special authority having powers to enact special regulations for the government and control of the harbour placed under its charge, unless and until application from such harbour commission or special authority to have this Part so apply shall have been received and granted by the Governor in Council. If such harbour commission or special authority is abolished the harbour may thereafter be proclaimed a public harbour under the provisions of section 849 of the act.
2.	Thait section 854 be amended so as to provide that the Governor in Counci, may make rules and regulations for the government of any public harbour or port in Canada, but in the case of any harbour or port to which Part XII does not aipply under the provisions of section 850 as amended, any such rule or regulation as may be inconsistent with any rule or regulation in force in any such harbour or port shall not be held to apply to the said har bour or port until application therefor from the harbour commission or other special authority shall have been received and granted by the Governor in Council.

Part XII of the
Canada Shipping Act gives power to the Governor in Council to appoint harbour masters and defines their duties. Section 850 states that certain ports are exempted from the provisions of Part XII, being the ports administered by harbour commissions. In such cases the harbour master is appointed by the harbour commissioners and is under their control, and the rules and regulations adopted by the Harbour Commission are followed. Since the passage of the Canada Shipping Act many new harbour commissions have been created by statute, and the purpose of the proposed legislation is to add to the exceptions stated in section 850 the additional harbours which are now under control of a harbour commission. It is
Canada Shipping Act

proposed aido to apply a similar exemption to ports which in the future may be placed under a harbour commission. Section 2 has practically the same purpose: when there is no harbour commission the rules and regulations adopted by the Governor in Council apply; when there is a harbour commission the regulations of the Governor in Council do not apply if they come in conflict with those of the commission. It is also provided that harbour commissions may at any time request that the general regulations of the Governor in Council should apply to their ports as well as to the others.
As I understand it, the theory is to place the control and management of the harbours entirely in the hands of harbour commissions, where they exist?
So far as the harbour master is concerned.
Subject only to the qualification that the port warden is to be appointed by the Government.

The duties of the
port warden do not relate to any of the functions of the harbour commission. The duty of the port warden, as of the shipping master, is to see to the enforcement of the Canada Shipping Act and the regulations of the Department of Marine. He must be under the Department of Marine; but the functions of harbour master are directly connected with those of the harbour commissioners.

The practice is then to leave the management of harbours to the harbour commissioners, aside from the offices referred to. Is any change made by this legislation from previous practice, and if so, to what extent?

The ports of Quebec, Montreal, Three Rivers, Toronto, Halifax, Pictou, and St. John were the only ports excepted from the provisions of Part XII of the Canada Shipping Act. We are adding to these the following ports now administered by a commission: Hamilton, Belleville, Vancouver, North Fraser, New Westminster, Winnipeg, St. Boniface. It is to give autonomy to these ports and place them on the same footing as the ports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax.

I understand that, but what I want to know is whether any change in practice is being made. I
[Mr. Lapointe. 1
have understood that these ports are already autonomous. I suppose my hon. friend thinks the law is not quite right, and by this legislation he seeks to remedy that?

No; as it is, the
harbour master is appointed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries; under the law as it will be, the harbour master will be appointed by and be under the control of the harbour commissioners.
Resolution reported,' read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 144, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Public Harbours and Harbour Masters).
Motion agreed to and bill read the first and second times, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

The purpose of this resolution is more especially to make more proportionate the fees paid for a cannery license and for a curing establishment license. It is also for the purpose of bringing about a better proportion between the fees paid by the smaller and the larger operators. The existing fee for a salmon curing establishment is $50. This is unfairly high for the small operator, and a very low fee for the big operator. For instance, the salmon cannery license is $500, plus four cents per case of 48 pounds of sockeye salmon put up, and three cents per case of all other varieties. Several salmon salteries in British Columbia put up over 100 tons of dry-salted salmon in a season, which would be equivalent to about 2,300 cases of canned salmon. Keeping in view the cost of operation involved, and the market for dry-salted salmon, it is considered that a fee of $1.25 per ton would compare fairly with the salmon cannery license.
The other change is to require a license for dry-salted herring. An important trade in dry-salted herring for the oriental market is now carried on in British Columbia. This business is largely in the bands of orientals. At the present time there is no license fee. It has been thought desirable that there should be a license, in order to allow the department to exercise proper supervision over these establishments. It is also considered that a fee similar to that required for salmon curing is reasonable, for while the product is worth less it costs very much less to produce and cure it. On the other hand we must do everything to encourage the pickling and canning of herring, as this means not only a much larger expenditure in the province, but a much better food product and a larger financial return for the country.
It is therefore proposed to exempt from a fee, bona tide operators who are seeking to develop the pickled and canned herring industry and \tfho are using the herring not fit for such purposes for dry salting. This canned and pickled herring industry in British Columbia is not in the hands of the people I have just mentioned, and there is not the same objection to exempting them from that fee. As I have already stated they use for the purpose only the herring that could not be canned in their industry. I know that this legislation has been asked for by almost everybody in British Columbia, and it has been represented that it is most unfair to the salmon canning industry that the salted salmon industry carried on by the orientals largely should not pay a fee at least equivalent to the fee paid by the salmon canners.

I would like
to ask the minister how the value of the dry salted salmon compares with that of the canned salmon?
I have not that information here but I can secure it for my hon. friend.

Never mind.
From what the minister says I would have thought that most of the business of putting down this dry salted salmon would be done in the smaller units but I see that he has fixed a tax of fifty cents a ton when the amount is only ten tons, and $1.25 when the production exceeds fifty tons. What is the idea of that?

I do not think anybody fears competition with the small operators. There are some people out there who really put up only a few tons of salmon, and under the present law they were paying $10 for their license. It was felt that that was really too high and that a smaller fee should be charged.

I agree with
that.

This provision is
rather to hit the larger operators who export to other countries.

But what is
the underlying idea of this graduated scale? Is it merely to assist the canned salmon operators, or is it something that has been scientifically worked out?

The idea is not to
make the burden heavy on the small opera-

Fisheries Act Amendment

tors, but to equalize it as between the larger operator in this industry and the operator in the canning industry.

With a view
of equalizing the cost of production?
Yes.

I would just like to ask
the minister about that last paragraph; I did not quite understand what he said. I gather that these fees will not apply to an establishment that is operating in the canned or pickled herring industry if it goes into the dry salting business. It does not pay any license in that case?

That is the meaning
of it.

Well then I would submit
that is hardly just. That will allow a canner, for instance, who is operating a cannery, presumably on a profitable basis, to compete with a man who does not own a cannery in the dry salting of salmon business. Why should that man be exempt from this taxation because he happens to own a cannery somewhere. It puts a direct premium upon the operations of the man who owns a cannery as against the very people the minister has been undoubtedly trying to help with his previous resolution-I refer to the small operator. The man who puts up ten tons will have to pay a license of fifty cents a ton, and so on, up to $1.25 and his product will have to compete with that of the man who happens to own a cannery somewhere in the province and who does not pay any fee on the salted herring. Is that the situation?

Well, he pays a high fee for his license but he would not pay for that side line, as my hon. friend says. He only uses the herring that cannot go into the canning industry. He does so in order that the product may not be lost altogether. We want to encourage the industry of pickling and canning herring. This provision is not directed against the same people as the rest of the section, as my hon. friend knows.

I do not know that there are many canners who can herring but here is the situation: We will say there are two men within twenty miles of each other. One is a canner and he makes money out of it or I suppose he would not run the establishment. He runs it for six months in the year and in the winter season uses
[Mr. Lapointe.!
the plant to put up dry salted salmon. He may put up 100 tons and yet pay no license fee for it whatever. His product competes with that of the man who is putting up solely this dry salted salmon. That does not appear to me to be equitable.
Of course a salmon canner has to pay a license; I do not think there is any cannery which specializes in the canning of herring.

I do not understand this resolution either in the way my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) understands it or in the way the minister understands it. I thought that this exception had nothing whatever to do with the canning or pickling of salmon but had to do with the canning or pickling of herring-
That is right.
-and that in so far as dry salted salmon was concerned they would have to pay whether they had canneries or not.
No it relates to herring.
So that the exception is for herring.
That is right.
The minister gave us a fee as to the salmon but he did not mention the fee paid by the canned or pickled herring industry. Do they pay fees?
I do not think they do as such, but it is always the salmon cannery that goes into the business of canning herring; there is no herring cannery.
Well, then, my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni was right in the point he was making because these pickled herring industries are really salmon industries.
Except that they are already paying a fee of $500 as salmon canners, and the others are not paying anything.
Let us make this clear. The only exception is as to herring?
Yes.

And there is no exception whatever as to the fees in the case of dry salted salmon whether it is a cannery or not; is that right?

Fisheries Act Amendment
Yes.

We will take the example of a man who has a cannery up in the Naas district, away up in the north of British Columbia; it may be that he happens to own that cannery, or it is owned by a big company. Why should they be favoured as against the man who confines himself to putting up dry salted salmon? Will the minister explain that? It is a direct advantage to the man or the company having a number of canneries; I cannot see what is the purpose of the provision enabling him to escape this tax.
He does not escape on dry salted salmon.

As far as I can understand it the situation is that although the salmon packing plants are the ones that do go into this herring business, in so far as the herring pickling activities of those plants are concerned they are only small. The minister desires to advance the herring industry and therefore makes no charge, in so far as the dry salted herring are concerned, provided the cannery is in the canning and herring pickling business. That is as I understand it.

On section 2-British Columbia herring curing establishments to have license; fees.
There is nothing to be gained by railroading things through. I think we should have time to look through the bill. I have not yet seen a copy.

Do I understand this

more severe penalty than has heretofore been imposed. My hon. friend (Mr. Stork) suggests deportation in the case of aliens. That is a matter for the consideration of the committee. speechtext:
The proposed changes in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act are, I believe, highly commendable, and as there is an evident desire to expedite business of the House, I do not propose to go into the subject at such length as I had originally intended to do.
Some hon MEMBERS: Hear, hear. Let us save time.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen say "hear, hear." If they will concur in the suggestions which I am about to make, the passage of this bill will be greatly facilitated. The amendments which the minister has brought down have, I think, the support of our people generally throughout the country. On the Coast large numbers of organizations such as those mentioned by the minister, boards of trade, community service clubs, and other bodies recently conducted an investigation into the drug traffic, and the appalling disclosures made caused them to urge very strongly upon the Government the amendments which are now incorporated in this bill, and others which are not so incorporated, and to the latter I will address myself in a moment.
In order that the House may understand the idea behind the movement in western Canada and other parts of the Dominion, I propose to read a resolution passed by the Vancouver Board of Trade which contains practically my 'argument on this subject. The Vancouver Board of Trade is one of the largest in Canada, and at a meeting held on the 7th February last, it passed this resolution:
"Whereas, the illegal sale and traffic in drugs or narcotics appears from an investigation by certain organizations in Greater Vancouver to have grown in this and other cities to an alarming extent, bringing in its wake degeneracy, crime and moral and physical ruin ,
And whereas, various service clubs and public bodies deem it expedient to arouse the public to the seriousness of the situation and necessity for remedial measures to prevent the existing illegal traffic and its increase;
It is, therefore resolved that this meeting of the Vancouver Board of Trade, strongly urges the proper authorities to immediately amend or alter the existing laws pertaining to the illegal sale and traffic in drugs in order to provide for the enforcement of the following remedies:
(a) The elimination of fines as a penalty for illegal selling of drugs or narcotics and the

Opium, and Narcotic Drugs
substitution therefore of a prison sentence of not less than one year and not more than ten years with lashes upon entering ar in the discretion of the magistrate upon leaving, for all cases;
(ib) And in addition to the prison sentence deportation for all aliens or those possible under the law; and in the case of those who under the law cannot be deported, they shall report periodically and for such time and to such person as the sentencing judge may determine; failure to report to incur further imprisonment or restraint in a proper public institution ;
(c) In the case of a naturalized alien convicted of selling, cancellation of naturalization papers and deportation after prison sentence.
Some of those suggestions are not embodied in these proposed amendments. I believe the minister was willing to introduce the penalty of deportation, and I strongly urge upon the Government the wisdom of including it in the bill. I believe that if a foreigner is convicted of illegally selling a drug-and many of these traffickers are foreigners-he should be deported; he is no good.in Canada. I beg to offer in amendment to subsection 2:
That after the word "summarily" in the fifteenth line of subsection 2 there shall be added the following words, "and shall at the discretion of the judge be liable to whipping."
Of course, I admit that that is a severe penalty. In the fifteenth line of this subsection there is the following proviso:
-Provided that any person who unlawfully sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any minor shall be proceeded against by indictment and not summarily.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I contend that the man who induces a minor to indulge in the drug habit should not be relieved from such a penalty as whipping. The chief purpose of such an amendment will not be so much in its application as in its deterrent effect upon those men who contemplate engaging in this traffic, for when they know that the law contains a priviso of that kind the dread of being subjected to the lash will effectually deter them from incurring the risk. I have examples here of the most monstrous action on the part of men engaged in this traffic, involving young girls of fifteen and sixteen. I say that if a man is convicted for perhaps the third time of selling these drugs to a girl of sixteen whom he has seduced and brought into the traffic, there should be power in the hands of the magistrates to have the lash applied. Some hon. members may think it ip too extreme a punishment, but for many other offences under the criminal code the application of the lash is provided, as, for instance, in the
case of rape, hold-up with intent to wound, and burglary. The effect of the carrying on of the drug traffic upon the moral qualities of manhood and womanhood is to bring about diseases of the vilest kind and crimes of all sorts-theft, murder, hold-up. The court records disclose the interesting fact that in the majority of cases the people engaged in these criminal enterprises are followers of the drug traffic. I have here a number of cases which were investigated by a responsible body of citizens in Vancouver and other cities. Out of the forty or fifty cases which I have before me I will take just one. A young girl of sixteen was brought before the committee and examined-and I may say that other inquiries were made with a view to determining the correctness of this evidence, which was established beyond any doubt. This girl is a morphine or cocaine addict, is afflicted with venereal disease, prostitutes with Chinamen. She is a resident of Vancouver and has been during her whole life. She acquired the habit through mixing with men engaged in the traffic. On the morning of the investigation she was engaged in this unfortunate pursuit in order to earn sufficient money, $5.50, to buy drugs to last her for the day. This traffic is carried on in a cool and calculating way. The men who sell the drug do not themselves use it; they know its terrible effects, but they exercise all their resourcefulness and ingenuity to induce others to acquire the habit. They have what are called " snow parties ", a kind of social entertainment in which they get the confidence of people and induce them to try the cocaine or whatever it may be. They dare them to try it, and by doing this again and again they ensure for themselves a market for their wares. I say it is not too much to ask that Parliament confer upon the judges trying these men the power to administer the lash, as is done in such other cases as I have mentioned. In fact, the effects of the drug traffic are even more serious than the consequences of the other crimes that I have referred to. I submit that the members of the committee should stand behind this amendment. It is sound in principle, and the result of its adoption would be to deter those who otherwise would be engaged in the traffic-in other words, to protect the young people of our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
By the bill which is now under consideration we provide more severe
Opium and Narcotic Drugs

penalties than have hitherto been applied in the case of those who carry on illicit trade in narcotics. Besides it is my intention to move a little later that all aliens convicted under this act shall be deported. The committee will have an idea of the effect of a deportation clause upon the traffic when I say that for the year ended September 30, 1921, there were in Canada 1,864 convictions, and of that number 1,211 were Chinese. So that if the amendment I propose becomes law and that number of Chinamen are affected, there would be 1,211 deportations. Of course, there would still be a number at large, but hon. members will admit that the remedy would be an effective one.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is there any record of how many of these Chinese were not naturalized?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have not the figures before me, but I understand that only a limited number of Chinamen are naturalized; from information which I have received, I understand that most of them are aliens. So far as the proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Ladner) is concerned, I know that the crime is a serious one. But the application of the lash has so far been confined to cases of physical crime, and it is a question whether it would be advisable to apnly that punishment in the case of convictions in connection with traffic in narcotic drugs. Possibly we should not adopt the provision embodied in my hon. friend's amendment, at least until we have seen, in the course of the next twelve months- what the result will be of the new provisions made for stricter punishment. Of course, I am in the hands of the committee in this respect, but I suggest that my hon. friend wait until next session before pressing his amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What proportion of the 1,211 Chinese could have been deported if the amendment which is to be proposed by the minister had been in effect last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni asked me the same question, and I replied that I was not in a position to say how many of these 1,211 were naturalized. I think that very few of them would be Canadians.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There might be
others. A great many of our Chinese in British Columbia come from Hong Kong and other British possessions. What would
rMr. Beland. ]
you do in a case of that kind? I am extremely doubtful if we would be able to deport a great number of these persons if convicted.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am surprised to hear that statement, because I took it for granted that the deportation provision would hit at the very heart of the trade amongst the Chinese.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think it is a good provision, but I do not know how it will work out.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Would the minister go so far as to say "or naturalized aliens"? I think that would meet the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that that would be a very unusual provision. The moment an alien becomes naturalized he is a Canadian, and I do not know but what it would be declared ultra vires.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would ask the minister, who is a medical man, if he does not consider that the extension of the drug traffic is a physical crime, because it brings about a physical disability that results in crime?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should just like to say a few words on this question. I have looked up the Hansard of last year, because I remembered that when this same question came up then, the then hon. member for Red Deer, myself, and some other medical men in the House at that time, including the minister, I think, were opposed to using the lash in cases of this kind on the general ground that it was hardly called for. However, I believe that the hon. gentlemen who represent British Columbia in this House are more familiar with this question than perhaps the rest of us, even those of us who are in the medical profession. I do not see, after all, that there would be any great harm, in fact, there might be a great deal of good, in accepting the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Vancouver South. While what the minister says is true that lashing should be kept for certain crimes of physical violence, I think perhaps moral violence as in this case is a much more serious crime. No one, however, understands the deplorable effects of the use of these habit-forming drugs better than the minister and myself, who are both members of the medical profession. I would ask the minister, with no desire to be contrary at all, to rec'onsider this amendment. I can see no real reason why the clause as drafted by the hon. member for

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
Vancouver South should not be accepted. It leaves it to the discretion of the judge to use this method of punishment. I believe that good would come of it. I cannot see how it would hurt the bill in any shape or form, and I therefore again appeal to the minister to reconsider, and insert this clause in the bill.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Before the minister replies, might I also point out to him one or two other matters? First, this extreme penalty of flogging is proposed to be applied to those traffickers who have been supplying drugs to minors. I wish the House could fully appreciate the horrible nature of this traffic. I know of no act that one human being could do to another more despicable and more fraught with utter depravity in its results than to supply these drugs to minors. We have seen so many, many cases that to us the traffic seems sickening, appalling. One would not dare to describe publicly the effects of these drugs. The minister gave the committee the number of convictions the other night. I think the two cities most seriously affected are Montreal and Vancouver, and perhaps Victoria, but Vancouver more particularly. Therefore, I say to the minister and to the House, that we might very well add this penalty of flogging in the case of traffickers convicted of selling drugs to minors. I might remind the House that I moved this amendment myself last year and the House very nearly accepted it. There was a pretty narrow division of opinion at that time, and I think it was my own inability to bring the matter strongly enough before the House that prevented the amendment from carrying.
Regarding the other point, I think that the clause the minister is adding providing for the deportation of aliens will very, very materially strengthen the bill and and the arm of the law. I also agree with him in his estimate that a very large proportion of these 1,200 Chinese would be aliens, and therefore subject to deportation. Comparatively few of these Chinamen would be naturalized. We may find it necessary in the working out of this provision, to strengthen it later on, but I wish to say to the minister with the utmost sincerity that we appreciate very much indeed his attempt to strengthen the bill, and we accord to him the highest commendation. I would ask him, however, and the House most earnestly to accept the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Vancouver South, and
add this .penalty of flogging in the case of those convicted of trafficking in drugs to minors.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has stated, there was a debate in the House on this question last year. At that time I opposed the principle of applying the lash, not only in this but in other cases, and I think the House was well advised in taking the stand it did on that occasion. I have not changed my views on that point since. I sympathize with the sentiments expressed by the minister. I think that we should first exhaust all other means of punishment before resorting to the lash. It does seem to me that we are reverting to the dark ages when we ask for that punishment of this kind be administered. I am sure that science and the brains of individuals to-day are capable of devising ways and means whereby this traffic which we all admit is one of the greatest evils extant in the country, could be eliminated without the application of the lash. I have no desire in any way to save individuals who may be convicted of this heinous crime, but I would plead along the line suggested by the minister, that we at least try out for a time the penalties proposed in the resolution offered by the minister before we endorse the sentiments expressed in the amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am sure we all very greatly appreciate the additions which the minister has made to the bill with regard to deportation. I quite understand, too, that it might be impossible to get rid of these orientals or foreigners who have become naturalized, but if we deport those who have been convicted of taking part in this traffic, I can readily see that we are moving in the direction of solving this oriental question.
There are certain points in discussing this matter which must not be overlooked. In the first place, very large profits are made out of this business, and consequently we have found in the past that these men will take almost any chance, and that they adopt the most ingenious methods for evading the law and carrying on this traffic. Again, we have another class of dealer who is himself subject to this habit, a man who take narcotics himself, and the strong desire to secure those narcotics and the high prices which they realize would induce that man to himself take any possible chances to obtain

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
money to buy drugs for his own use. Now, I cannot understand any argument which proposes to give any quarter to a trafficker in narcotics, particularly to one who supplies narcotics to a minor. I have been shown through some of these opium dens in British Columbia and the sights are simply appalling. Take the effects of the narcotics as described by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). There are hundreds of these cases out there, the traffic is increasing very rapidly, and I feel that we are quite justified in adopting any measure whatever that will overcome this traffic before it gains any further headway. Even if by the application of the lash, in cases where the magistrate thinks it is necessary, we can save only one or two persons during the coming year I think we should adopt the required measures right now and not postpone the legislation for another year. I think it is generally acknowledged by those who have been keeping close tab on this traffic that fine and imprisonment have not been nearly so effective as we thought these penalties would be when the law was first applied.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I also would like to support the amendment, but before dealing with it I would say that I think the minister's action in providing for the deportation of aliens who are convicted of this crime, is most commendable and I congratulate him on having gone that far. At the same time deportation will not cover all the offenders. Even on the figures that were given, if all the Chinese could be deported, that would cover only 1,200 out of 1,800 and would leave some 600 not subject to deportation. Now, what is going to happen to them? These people will pay a fine without any hesitation; they can afford to do so because there is a very large profit made in this traffic. I have had a good deal of experience in connection with the administration of the criminal law and I know that there are men who will take imprisonment with a smile on their face-that imprisonment does not seem to have a great deal of effect in a great many cases. But where a man is faced with a sentence that will subject him to whipping I have seen the most hardened criminals cringe, and I say it is the greatest deterrent that could possibly be placed in the Criminal Code. This crime, to my mind, is even more serious than the crime of robbery with violence. To hold a man up at the point of a gun and take his money
[Mr. Totalled
away from him is serious of course, but it is not so serious as to give drugs to a minor and take away his future. To render that minor an addict to the drug habit is the most terrible thing that could happen to him or to her. I would much rather have anyone hold me up, and shoot me for that matter, than sell me drugs and cause me to become a drug addict. I have seen the effects of this traffic; it is a terrible thing. We are not going too far when we give a judge discretion to order a lashing in what he considers to be an extreme case. I would press that view on the minister. I know he is trying to do his very best to meet the situation, I know that he appreciates its gravity, not only in places like Vancouver where investigations have been held, but elsewhere throughout Canada. In all the cities and towns of the Dominion this condition exists to a greater or lesser extent. Even here in the city of Ottawa the police could give information which would open the eyes of anyone who is nor acquainted with the facts. If we knew what was happening, if we knew what the true conditions were here in Ottawa-and in every city in Canada for that matter- I do not think we would hesitate for a moment in supporting this amendment. I know what it means to have a provision of this kind in the act, and I am convinced that if these traffickers knew that they would be lashed if they were convicted the traffic would be stopped to a very great extent.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not in a position to express very clear opinions based upon personal knowledge with regard to this traffic, but it is quite evident that the hon. members who represent our Pacific coast province have come into close contact with the trade, or into such close contact with it that we ought to be impressed by the representations they have made. In order that the committee may form some idea of the extent to which the traffic has gone I might give some figures that I saw this evening in the Literary Digest. The statement was there made that the United States was using ten times the amount of opium that European countries are using and the figures given were these: That 270 tons of crude opium, which would produce thirty-one tons of morphine, were imported into the United States, whereas one ton was sufficient to take care of the legitimate needs of the country. Now I do not know whether those figures are correct or not, but evidently the writer of tb$

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
article knew something about the matter; and if the situation is anything like as serious as that writer contends then it seems to me that no steps that we can take can be too strong to put'a stop to the traffic. I know the tendency of penal legislation in the present day, is, perhaps, towards more moderate methods than have been pursued in the past, and yet in this particular case it does seem to me that no steps which we can take can be too strong to prevent the degradation and the corruption of the young people of our land.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I see that the amendment reads:
-and shall at the discretion of the judge, he liable to whipping.
I also understand that this amendment is to apply exclusively to traffickers who sell to minors. My impression at first was that the penalty of the lash was to be applied in every case coming under subsection 1 of section 5 which we are now considering. However, it is proposed to be applied only to traffickers who sell, or furnish, or give narcotics to minors, and the punishment is to be administered at the discretion of the judge. I have an open mind on the question. I know that the traffic must be suppressed if at all possible. My hon. friend a moment ago referred to the fact that perhaps the people of the East were not fully in possession of the facts, were not fully aware of how serious the situation was. But the traffic, as my hon. friend knows, is very large in the city of Montreal. I have received a personal letter from one of the most- eminent, I would call him-magistrates of the city stating that the traffic in Montreal has reached very large dimensions, and that .the situation had to be met in the most severe manner. I call the attention of the House to the fact that, in the United States, the laws with regard to narcotic drugs do not provide for the application of the lash. They provide for very severe penalties in fines and imprisonment, and also for the deportation of aliens, but, as far as whipping is concerned, they do not inflict it. I am in the hands of the House, and if the committee decide the amendment should carry, I am willing to incorporate it in the bill.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I desire to support the
proposed amendment offered by the hon. member for Vancouver Sou h (Mr. Ladner). I think flogging is quite proper in
a case of this kind, where the crime is coolly premeditated. I think it is entirely in order, and the provision will probably not be abused if it is left to the discretion of the judge.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Referring to conditions in the city of Montreal for the last few years, I desire to concur in all that the minister has said. A recent report published a few weeks ago by the Chief of Police, Mr. Belanger, attributed to foreigners the responsibility for, perhaps, 75 per cent of the crime committed in the city of Montreal. On Lagauchetiere street, in that city, and in that district we have a Chinatown, many houses have been converted into Chinese dives, and raids on the opium dens are a daily occurrence. The illicit sale of opium, cocaine and other drugs has become a terrible nuisance, and must be put down. It is worse than a nuisance, it has become a crime. I remember one case, in particular, where $35,000 worth of opium was seized when a raid was made, and brought down to the police court, to be exhibited in court, if necessary It was left in the police station, but the station was broken into and the opium was stolen. The traffic is ten times worse than ihe liquor traffic. The people engaged in this drug business are in the worst business, and no penalty is too severe to fit the crime. I think the most severe punishment is absolutely necessary, because the paying of the money penalty is nothing to these people, who make large sums out of the traffic. I will strongly support the amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With regard to the
application of the lash, I would like to bring before the committee the method of carrying out the sentence. If you say that a man has to pay $100 fine, we know exactly what it is. When we say he has to spend two years in penitentiary, we understand what it means. We have a trained judge to measure out the penalty, either imprisonment or fine, but when we say that a man shall receive ten, twenty of fifty lashes, who is going to administer them? We have no officials who are trained for that purpose and who understand what the lash means. The great country to the south of us has not adopted the principle of administering the lash.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
They have lynch
law.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Lynch law is an outrage on civilization. No country cares to

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
adopt it, it has no statutory approval or sanction, and is only applied where the people take the law into their own hands. Now, who is going to apply the lash? There cannot be any uniformity about it. The lash depends upon the strength, the character and the nature of the man in whose hands it is operated. I bring this matter to the attention of the committee, so that they will know why there is such a reluctance in the country about imposing this penalty. Last year' this matter was put before us in another shape, and we were asked by the Minister of Justice to pass a law by which young boys, instead of being imprisoned, should receive flogging or lashing, and the House was unanimously against it. It received no quarter at all. If deportation and fiines or imprisonment will meet the case, I am with hon. members at every turn, but I am opposed to the frightful brutality of the lash, when you put it in the hands of a man who has had no training in administering it. You know what a dollar is, and what imprisonment is, but you do not know what a lash is. It may have no appreciable effect at all. I hope that we shall be able to carry out criminal laws to the extreme, without using the lash.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am surprised at the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie)-although undoubtedly it was not done purposely-creating the impression that the lash would be indiscriminately used. The Criminal Code provides distinctly the method by which it shall be applied. It says that the Convicted person shall, first, be examined by a doctor to ascertain whether he is in a condition to receive the lash. It shall be a cat o' nine tails. It shall be applied by a certain official of the penitentiary, and, if he is not available, by a man appointed by the Justice Department. The most careful provision is made in the law for the application of the lash. It is applied in many cases, and this would only be applying a principle of justice now in practice.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I wish to add what
small weight my local knowledge will furnish in favour of the amendment. While	I understand all	that can
be said against the principle of flogging-people say it is out of date and brutalizing, and so it is-I fully belieVe the conditions justify its use, and no one who has not lived in the West can understand the conditions. While flogging may be un-

pleasant for the party, think of the living hell these young people are sentenced to by reason of the use of these drugs, mot for an hour or two or a month or two, but for all their lives, and, perhaps, for eternity. Some 60 or 70 years ago there was ah epi-dtmic of garrotting in London, England, and it spread to a tremendous extent. It was easily done. A foot pad came behind a man and twisted a cord or shawl around the man's neck, and he was either rendered insensible or choked to death. It was difficult to detect, because it was so easily done, and no evidence was left. It went on to a remarkable extent, and people were terrified to go out after dark. Where the victims were not killed, and the garrotters were convicted, the judge gave the lash, and inside of three months the practice totally ceased. You will find in some of the treatises on criminal codes, how speedily that simple application of the lash absolutely caused that practice to cease. These men who are capable of committing these low, beastly crimes, are afraid of their own skin. Very often, when a man is going to be hanged, he asks, not in regard to his future, but "Will it hurt?" and they suffer perhaps more from the thought of being lashed than from the idea of being hanged. The situation in British Columbia fully justifies this amendment.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Subsection 2 (a) reads:
Any person who manufactures, imports, exports, sells or distributes any drug and neglects or refuses to keep the record required, etc.
Does that apply to physicians in the country? Have they to keep records?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I move two amendments. The first has reference to the appeal that can be taken under the present law from a judgment of the inferior court to the higher court. I am prompted to submit this amendment by reason of a personal communication which has reached me from an important magistrate in the city of Montreal, and which convinces me that

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
these appeals should be restricted to cases where legal points are in dispute. I do not want to delay the committee but I shall read a few paragraphs from this letter. The letter is personal and I shall not give the name of the writer:
It was called upon to preside at the sessions of the Court of King's Bench in appeal against decisions of lower courts of criminal jurisdiction, and I think it is my duty to place .before you certan suggestions which came to my mind in the course of the hearings of these cases.
Out of 76 cases inscribed for appeal, 60 of them at least were cases where the appellant had been condemned by the lower court for having been found in possession of drugs, such as cocaine, morphine or opium, or for having sold or purchased drugs, or for having visited places where such drugs are supplied.
In most cases the charge was upheld. The accused flies an appeal, either in order to obtain sufficient delay to enable him to find the sum which he has to pay as a penalty, or in order to postpone his imprisonment in cases where he is condemned to serve a term in jail. In both cases the accused hopes that his solicitor will find irregularities in the wording of the charge, or in the sentence or in other procedures, through which he might obtain his discharge.
I may slate that I did not "fall" for the clever arguments of lawyers on technicalities.
Abuse is being made of the right to appeal. If you knew, Sir, the shameful traffic of drugs which is carried on in Montreal '. Young men and very young girls are enticed into supposed-to-be honest places of amusement, and, under the pretext of experimentation, drugs are served to them as wine would be. The law can never be too severe on the traffickers and distributors of drugs.
Further on the writer says:
I believe, Sir, that you would render an immense service to the community if you were to make the law as severe as possible against those engaged in this ignominious trade.
He concludes by asking that appeals should be restricted. I therefore move, as section 5, the following:
The said act is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 10 thereof:
(10a) : Sections 749 to 760, inclusive, of the Criminal Code shall not apply to any conviction, order or proceeding in respect of any offence under this act.
I am informed by the Minister of Justice that these sections mentioned refer only to appeals from decisions of lower courts in criminal cases. Section 761 of the Criminal Code provides for an appeal on any stated case on a point of law. I do not think there can be objection to the proposed amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I suppose the minister has carefully considered this matter, but it seems to me that it introduces a dangerous principle into our jurisprudence. I have every possible sympathy with this act and
the way in which it has been amended to make the punishments for this crime as severe as possible. I have no sympathy with merely technical appeals; and yet the right to appeal, the right to have a sentence reviewed is, I think, inherent in the administration of justice as we know it. A man should not be wrongly punished. After all, the great feature of Magna Charta was that no man should be imprisoned or executed without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land. And when you say that not merely an irregularity but something worse may exist and there shall be no remedy, I think you are going to a very dangerous length. Bad as may be the crime for which this act provides punishment, it cannot be worse than many other crimes that are punished by the law. Yet it has always been the boast of our jurisprudence that the meanest criminal has the right to be heard and the right to the punctual observance of all the forms of law. I do not contend for a moment that the form should override the substance, but there are so many formal errors that are now cured by the Criminal Code that nothing is left except matters of a rather substantial character. It seems to me therefore, that we ought not unduly to smooth the path for magistrates who will not prepare themselves or who are careless in the exercise of g their jurisdiction. In the cities where this class of crime will be principally dealt with there is no excuse for slothfulness or bungling on the part of magistrates, and I have no sympathy with weak appeals from magistrates who either do not know their duty or are too careless to observe the sanctions which the law has framed, not for the purpose of allowing the guilty to escape, but of preventing the innocent from suffering. The old saying, "It is better that ninety-nine men should escape than that one innocent man should suffer" is outworn. But our Criminal Code has destroyed the great bulk of the old technical objections, and I would ask the minister to consider very carefully before he introduces this new principle into our law. It cannot be necessary if competent men are adequately discharging their functions. Once in a rare while you will have someone blundering, but it will not be so ordinarily. It is all very well to say that there may be an appeal by a reserved case, but why should the ordinary right of appeal be denied for this particular class of crime when it applies so generally to other Classes? We
Opium and Narcotic Drugs

do not want a man to be convicted except according to the law. The principle involved is a great deal wider than the mere scope of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I appreciate very much indeed the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John. I surmise that he was not in his seat when I read the letter which I received from one of the magistrates in the city of Montreal who lately sat in appeal there on several of these cases.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I saw the minister
reading something, but the conversation going on in the Chamber prevented me from hearing him.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The learned magistrate stated that out of 76 cases inscribed for appeal before him 60 were cases where the appellant had been condemned by a lower court for trafficking illegally in drugs. He contends, and I think he is justified, that appeal in most cases is taken in order to gain time and find the money wherewith to pay the fine and escape imprisonment. Wealthy traffickers come to the rescue of their poorer friends and supply the money. The magistrate also said: "In order to obtain satisfactory results from the severe sentences imposed, it would be necessary to take away the right of appeal as it has been done in the case of disorderly houses." The principle is not a new one, at least so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, where there is no appeal in the case of conviction for keeping a disorderly house. This provision. I think, is one more weapon in the hands of the Government in its efforts to suppress the drug traffic, and that was the object I had in view when I introduced the amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Strange as it may seem, Mr. Chairman, I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for St. John! I think there are two kinds of cases to be taken into consideration. My recollection is that if in the case of a disorderly house the conviction is by way of what is known technically as "summary conviction" there is a right of appeal; but there is no such right in the event of conviction by a. police magistrate. Now, a police magistrate in most of our large cities has a jurisdiction which is substantially the same as that of a district or county court judge. But this bill gives the power of conviction to an ordinary justice of the peace, a man who is not specially trained, and who perhaps is not accustomed to weighing carefully the

value of evidence; yet this justice of the peace is given the power to take away the liberty of the individual for a period of six months in addition to imposing a fine. I think it is highly desirable that in cases of this kind where the conviction is by way of summary proceedings there should be a right of appeal. The letter read by the minister indicates that even in the city of Montreal, where there is a trained judge trying the cases at the outset, some appeals were allowed. It seems to me that the appeal right should not be taken away where convictions under this Act are made by ordinary justices of the peace.
In the act as it stands I presume that no imprisonment can be imposed, because the Montreal judge suggested that those convicted commenced appeal proceedings for the purpose of gaining time to pay their fines; but under this bill it is obligatory on the court to impose imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. It is not obligatory in all cases. Those licensed to sell drugs may upon conviction for breaches of the act be condemned either to pay a fine or go to gaol; but illicit traffickers must be condemned to imprisonment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I accept the minister's statement. In the event of appeal the minister is aware that the accused person must put up security to the satisfaction of a district court judge, and must take other steps in order to prosecute his appeal within a limited time. I see no objection to allowing an appeal. I do not see how any one is going to be prejudiced, and it maybe that only in a few cases will the sentence be reversed, but it is important in those cases that justice be done, and therefore I think we should hesitate about taking away from any person his right of appeal. The minister suggests that the person convicted has a right to appeal by way of a case stated, so called; but in such an event there is no deliberation by the appellate body to consider the weight to be given to the evidence, the only matter under consideration is a point of law, and consequently even in that event injustice may be done to the accused.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I heartily concur in most that has been said by the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for St. John. I think it behooves us to be very careful in taking away from the citizen any right which will insure him justice. Many of the magistrates who try these cases by way of procedure known as summary ecmvic-

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
tion are absolutely unskilled in the law and do not know anything at all about the admissibility of evidence. There cannot be, as mentioned, an appeal by way of a case stated, where the ordinary right of appeal is taken away by the special statute under which the conviction is made. An examination of the Criminal Code will show that in cases of summary conviction Parliament has gone as far as it could go toward removing the defendant's right of certiorari except where there is a want of jurisdiction in the magistrate. It used to be the right of the accused-the right has now been almost entirely taken away -that a person could bring about a review of a magistrate's decision by a writ of certiorari. If the conviction was bad, and a person was confined to gaol he could obtain a writ of habeas corpus and a writ of certiorari in aid of habeas corpus in order that the evidence might be reviewed for the purpose of seeing whether the conviction was a proper one or whether there was sufficient evidence to support it. In the province of Nova Scotia it was held in the case of the Queen vs. Walsh that when a matter was brought up by way of certiorari it was not competent for the courts to go into the evidence; in fact, they were not permitted to look at the evidence at all if the conviction was complete and regular on its face. Other provinces, however, held that when a matter was brought up on certiorari, the court dealing with the writ of certiorari had a right to look at the evidence. There was, therefore, this conflict of decision. But a short time ago the Law Lords who are the judicial committee of the House of Lords held that the Nova Scotia court was right in the case of the Queen vs. Walsh; so that the law as regards certiorari was really established by the Nova Scotia decision in the case to which I have referred. So that now with the Criminal Code taking away as far as it can the right of certiorari, save where there is an absolute want of jurisdiction, and with the taking away of the right of appeal as now proposed, you are putting the defendant, in many cases, entirely in the hands of ignorant magistrates. I submit that the department is not running any risk by leaving where it is the right of appeal so that a man may have his case as tried by the magistrate determined de novo by a higher court. There should be no tendency in any way to derogate in any way from the rights of the individual. At any rate, in most of our laws we are
putting upon the defendant the burden of proving himself innocent rather than letting the Crown prove him guilty. If we persist in amending our laws in such a way that these rights are taken from the people, we shall soon come to a condition under which a man who is accused of a crime, whether there is bona fide reason for the charge or not, will be obliged to prove his own innocence rather than have his guilt established by the prosecution. We should jealously guard the rights of the individual. We should be very cautious in taking away the right of appeal, the only protection the defendant has, particularly when he is tried by magistrates who, as happens in many cases, are incompetent. iSo long as I occupy a seat in this House I shall by my voice and vote uphold the principle that the defendant in an action shall not be deprived of any of his rights; that he shall at least have extended to him the old presumption of British law that he is innocent until proven guilty. When the department ask for an amendment to take away from the subject rights which he has always had, it seems to me that they are getting lazy and do not want to take the trouble of obtaining the proper evidence to make convictions; they rather wish to act as a sort of autocratic body.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would like to add a word in support of the minister on this question. I think that too much emphasis has been laid upon the innocent man being deprived of all his rights and privileges and being made the subject of czarism and autocracy. That is not the principle of the minister's suggestion. The man who is affected in this case has the right of appeal in law.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: You are taking it away from him.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No; we are taking it away in relation to the facts.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is not the magistrate the judge of the facts as well as of the law? Has not the judge on appeal the . right to treat the whole thing de novo?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend misses the point of my contention. The question of appeal relates to the right of appeal on a point of law, and that would necessarily involve the facts as brought out before the magistrate. In most cases the facts are brought out at the trial before the magistrate, and even if some facts are
Opium and Narcotic Drugs

omitted there is always, under the Criminal Code, the right, in the case of error or the discovery of new evidence, to adduce the facts in question, so that there would really be no prejudice to the defendant. The amendment suggested by the minister would greatly aid in carrying out the spirit and purpose of this law, which is to down the traffic, not to give protection to those engaged in it.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I must protest against a government which is uplifting morals by legislation. My hon. friend (Mr. Ladner) says there is always the right of appeal under the Criminal Code, but if the legislation proposed by the minister becomes law, there is no appeal. I take the ground that every person is entitled to an appeal from the magistrate to a county or district or superior court judge, and if the legislation proposed by the minister goes through, that right is denied him. We have the same thing in liquor legislation; in our province a man who is convicted of an offence against the prohibition act may not take an appeal. It simply means that the magistrate may convict on very slender evidence or no evidence at all, and if he does, there is no appeal from the facts, no right to take the case to a superior court judge. There is always, of course, the right of certiorari, of which the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) has spoken, and the right of habeas corpus. But if the Government or friends of the Government take the stand that a man should be prohibited from taking appeal, it looks to me like poor legislation. It looks to me as if the government were taking a stand on a question the soundness of which there were doubtful of. It looks to me as if they are putting the machinery of the law in this country into the hands of magistrates, who, as the hon. member for Hants has said, very often misconduct trials-I know it is so in my province. There should be no such thing as depriving a man of the right to appeal, a right which, my hon friend will perhaps say, is statutory-a right which is as old as the statutes themselves. I know that the min' ister is legislating in respect to a very serious matter, and I hope that through the legislation he is bringing in he will be able to put the traffic in drugs and intoxicating liquors and that of thing out of business. But I think he would be well advised to put that kind of illegal traffic out of business by means which are sanctioned under our constitution, and which
fMr. Ladner.]
have been handed down to us in the British system of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that in the case of prosecutions for the sale of liquor in the province of Quebec, there have never been any appeals?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: 'So much the worse for the province of Quebec, and so much the worse for the people who legislate in that direction. We have no appeals in the province of Nova Scotia, hut two wrongs do not make a -right, and I for my part protest, and protest most vigorously, against that sort of legislation, whether in the province of Quebec or any other province.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend from St. John stated that there might be an appeal by way of a stated case, but I find that subsection 2 of section 769 of the Criminal Code provides:
Where, toy any special act, it is provided that there shall be no appeal from any conviction or order, no proceeding's shall be taken to have a case stated or signed as aforesaid in any case to which such provision as to appeal in such special act applies.
So if there is no appeal provided for in this special act, there is no right to appeal by way of stated case.
Amendment agreed to.

On motion of Sir Lomer Gouin (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 107 to amend the Bankruptcy Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On Section 2-Notice of Suspension of Payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I informed the House in introducing the bill the amendments proposed are not of a substantial character. This legislation is to dispose of certain doubts which have arisen as to the meaning of certain provisions and to provide for a more expeditious and satisfactory enforcement of the act. The first amendment seeks to add to the grounds on which a debtor may be adjudicated bankrupt. At present a creditor in order to force the debtor to turn over his assets to a trustee has first to take action against him, get judgment, and have an execution issued. After that lengthy, and sometimes
expensive, course, if the execution is not satisfied, after a delay of fourteen days, application can be made to the judge on bankruptcy for a receiving order. Business men all over the country have represented to us that it is very difficult for them to prevent a debtor from disposing of assets during litigation. It appears to me that if a debtor gives notice to any of his creditors that he has suspended, or is about to suspend payment of his debts, the creditors should be entitled to petition the court for a receiving order. Similarly, if he ceases to meet his liabilities as they become due, he is to all intents and purposes insolvent, and the court should have jurisdiction to deal with his assets for the benefit of his creditors accordingly. That principle is already embodied in our Winding Up Act, and it was in the Insolvency Act of 1875. We have been requested as I have said, by the business men of Canada to adopt this amendment and I hope the House will consent to this being done.

Section agreed to.
On Section 3-Avoidance of general assignment of book debts:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 30 of the statute, which it is proposed to amend, provides in effect for the avoiding of general assignments of book debts. It was the intention of Parliament to prevent a debtor from giving preference to certain creditors by means of a secret assignment of book debts. Different cases were brought to court and it was decided, especially in Ontario, that even in the provinces where there was no such registration provided by law assignments were not avoided. A contrary decision was rendered in Nova Scotia, and it is in order to dispose of that doubt that we propose to amend the law and ask to have the section read as it is found in the bill. We make it very clear that the principle is that assignments are to be avoided, and we make special exception only for provinces where they have legislation providing for registration.

If I understand the minister aright the effect of this amendment is that in provinces where there is no provision for the registration of an assignment of book debts, the assignment will not be permitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Section agreed to.
