I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a matter of great importance. I have reference to the establishment of a steamship service between the Atlantic and Pacific Canadian ports. There are certain classes of cargo which it does not pay at all to ship across the continent by rail. One of these is lumber. It is true we do ship by rail into Ontario a good deal of lumber of the more expensive kind, but the rate is so high that it is almost prohibitive. Large quantities of southern pine are also imported into that province. By the establishment of a steamship service we could ship cargoes of lum-

Steamship Services
ber around by the Panama canal route to Toronto. Indeed, I think we shipped twenty or thirty million feet to Toronto for harbour works within the last few years, which shows the feasibility of such a service. The difficulty is that we have not a regular steamship service. There is another matter that I would bring to the attention of the minister (Mr. Kobb), and also to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy, Essex), under whose department the operation of the steamships no doubt comes. The service from the Atlantic to the Pacific ports would touch the West Indies and points in Mexico. It could take traffic from eastern Canada to those ports, picking up cargoes through the West Indies and in Mexico and carrying them to the Pacific coast, and the reverse on the return trip. We have a market in the West Indies for many of our commodities, such as fish of all classes, and canned goods, lumber, shingles and, when we can get space, hay and oats. And there are many classes of goods that we require from the West Indies and from Mexico. I believe our various commercial bodies are strongly of the opinion that a service of this kind is necessary. The difficulty up to about a year or so ago has been the lack of shipping facilities; there were not sufficient vessels. That is not the case to-day. Now there are more than we have use for. There was, I believe, a question in the mind of the management of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine that we ought to demonstrate beyond any doubt that the cargoes were there. That is not the way in which steamship services are to be established on new routes. I should like to see the minister put on a regular service for a while. He has some vessels of 5,000 ton register and he might give one or two of them a chance to prove their usefulness. I recall an objection that was raised to the effect that this would be taking traffic from the railways. I do not think this objection is sound. The freight on the railway from coast to coast is so exceedingly high that, except in the case of package freight, the railways would not be affected by such a steamship service at all. From the eastern states a great deal of freight is shipped into the Pacific province by the American railways. We get none of the haulage in Canada at all. A lot of that freight could be picked up by these vessels at New York, and that would not only be helping the marine but it would at the same time be extending the trade of the country. I 192
would urge this matter very strongly upon the minister's attention.
Would the hon. member suggest that a subsidy be paid to the line he proposes?

At the moment I am not suggesting a subsidy. I suggest, however, that the Government might use one or two or more of their idle ships many of which are now lying, I understand, in the port of Montreal. If any hon. member thinks that the proposal is not a wise one, let me inform the committee that the Pacific end of the Government Merchant Marine has been fairly successful. We have had very excellent results from its operation on the Pacific and if we opened up the route I suggest I have no doubt it would be successful and would ultimately pay well.
Are there any vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine calling at ports that are now being served by the steamships that are subsidized by the Government, or at neighbouring ports?
Not regularly.
Do they sometimes call at those ports?
They have done so occasionally.
In other words, I take it, we have a steamship line subsidized by the Government operating in competition with the Canadian Government Marine.
The reverse is right.

My hon. friend (Mr. Garland) , who is a new member of t'he House, is probably not aware that we entered into a trade arrangement with the West Indies which provided for a subsidized service with certain equipment for carrying the products of the West Indies to Canada and for the transportation of mails to and from the Mest Indies. If my hon. friend has looked into the question he must know that Canada enjoys a considerable percentage of customs preference with the West Indies, with which she is developing an increasing trade. It was because of that increasing trade that within the past year Or so the Canadian Merchant Marine management put their boats on to get some of the business that had been worked up by subsidized lines-lines started many years be-



Steamship Services
fore we had a merchant marine. Indeed, we have had complaints from this subsidized line that unless we call off the Canadian government service their boats would be unable to continue the (Service at the subsidy we were giving them. It is important that we should retain that subsidized service because of the trade we enjoy. We have made no attempt to interfere with the work of the Canadian Merchant Marine. Our vessels were no't built for passenger service1, and the service we have agreed to establish between the West Indies and Canada calls for reasonably good passenger accommodation.
Regarding the point raised by my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), I know that he has taken a great deal of interest in it, and has made representations to the Government, and we are alive to the importance of giving the project very careful consideration. The opening up of the Panama canal introduces new channels of trade as between the East and the West. I am not prepared to-night to say what the policy of the Governinent will be; it is more a matter for consideration by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Kennedy), but I think the Government will take into consideration the representations made by my hon. friend, and if the line should look profitable, something may result.

Being a new member, Mr. Chairman, I have not yet become accustomed to the delightful sarcasm of my hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I protest against the continuation of this subsidy of $340,000 odd to a steamship line between Canada and the West Indies when we have a merchant marine some of which are already engaged on this route. The minister mentioned that our boats cannot be used in this service because they are not equipped with passenger accommodation. I understand that when the matter came up in the House last year Sir George Foster, the then Minister of (Trade and 'Commerce, stated that two of our boats had been equipped with passenger accommodation.
I might also call the (attention of the minister to the fact that last year, when in opposition, the present Solicitor General i Mr. McKenzie) took exception to the continuation of this subsidy. The remarks he made on that occasion are not very long, and I shall quote them. After stating that he

agreed very heartily with the point raised by Mr. Sinclair, he said:
The ipoint made by my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) is perfectly clear. We have an item of $340,366.60 for a line to the West Indies and South America. Now, we are told that we have our own boats serving a part of that route, so that we are in competition with the vessels running there. Yet the Government is so exceedingly generous that it gives to a company with whom it is competing for trade the sum of $340,000 odd. They gLve them that magnificent handicap and then boldly and proudly step up and say: We will get plenty of profit notwithstanding this handicap we are giving them. Does it strike my hen. friend as good business that we should be spending $75,000,000 of the people's money in the building of boats and in looking for trade and then when we find an old service established on this route which we intend to work, instead of trying to displace those competitors, give them a subsidy?
I sincerely trust that the Solicitor General has not altered his mind on this question, and I hope to get some support from him in my opposition to this particular item.
With regard to the contention raised by the minister that this subsidy was necessary because of the extent of our trade with the West Indies, I find that up to the end of the fiscal year, 1922, our import trade amounted to $8,113,000, while in 1917 it was $14,239,000. In fact, the figures received from the department indicate that there has been a falling off in our trade with the West Indies since 1917 to the extent of $6,125,000. If we take 1918 and compare the figures with this year we observe a falling off of $2,437,000. In the export trade there is a deficiency of about $4,000,000 over last year. I am not comparing the figures for this year alone with those for last year alone, because I agree with the contention-which no doubt will be raised-that last year was an exceptionally bad year, there being a great depression in the sugar industry and a consequent falling off in the value of the imports from the West Indies. But going back to 1917 and 1918, you find an appalling falling off of that business. There are reasons for that decline, Mr. Chairman. I believe that the British Undersecretary for the Colonies, Mr. Wood, is about to pay a visit to the West Indies to endeavour to co-ordinate their trade relations with other countries. It seems that at the present time there are-I do not know how many governments down there, but there are quite a large number of them; for instance, the Leeward Islands, the Windward Islands, British Honduras,

Steamship Services
the Bahamas, and so on, are all under separate governments, have separate trade regulations and different tariffs-
I am sorry to say, Mr. Chairman, that they have actually got tariffs down there. Mr. Wood is of the opinion that trade with the British West Indies is a matter of great difficulty, that it must be done in small parcels, in many cases hardly worth handling, particularly in view of the additional fact that as one of the direct results of this lack of co-operation no adequate shipping arrangements exist either between the United Kingdom and her Caribbean Colonies or between the Islands themselves. We are endeavouring to establish something in the way of shipping arrangements with the West Indies, but I would call the minister's attention to the fact that there are no adequate shipping arrangements between these different islands. In short, when a ship goes down to pick up a cargo it has to jump from one place three or four hundred miles to another place; there is no such thing as co-operation for trade purposes.
I might also call the minister's attention to the fact that the board of directors of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in their report last year refer to the West Indies service on which they have boats and state:
It must be remembered in connection with this service that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are pioneers in opening up a new route with a view to developing and extending Canada's trade. As it has been the practice of many governments to supplement the earnings of companies engaged in this work, and as steamship subsidies are paid by the Dominion Government for services that are much more remunerative than this West Indies service, it would only be reasonable that your company should be guaranteed against loss when engaged as in this case, in opening up a new route at the request of the Government.
The Canadian Merchant Marine is now appealing for subsidies, Mr. Chairman! There might have been some excuse for granting subsidies in the old days before we had our own merchant marine, but I submit that the practice should now cease. The minister raises the point that our merchant marine cannot be equipped for passenger service, but Sir George Foster says it can, and that two of the boats are already so equipped. They can also be equipped for cold storage. At the present time our trade with the West Indies must oniy be a summer trade, for we have no warehousing facilities for a winter trade; but it has been recently suggested that there
should be in South America, at a point of call on the way back from the West Indies, warehousing facilities established so you could take in your West Indian trade during the winter as well as summer. I call the minister's attention to one other remark made by Mr. Stollmeyer, speaking at a meeting of the Agricultural Society in Trinidad. He said:
We have in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine a means of transport which needs encouragement.
I heartily agree with the statement of that gentleman; it needs encouragement, and we might encourage it. The attitude of the Canadian manufacturers has, unfortunately, a great deal to do with the difficulty of this trade. It seems to be very difficult to get return cargoes.
Carried.

My hon. friends seem to be in a hurry; they always are when we touch the manufacturers. Mr. Jones, president of the Canada Cement Company, whom the manufacturers will have a great deal of respect for, lately returned from South America. Discussing an address that had been made with regard to trade with South America and the West Indies, he sai:
What struck me most forcibly was the one
sided view Canadian business men took on thes questions of import and export.
You cannot expect the West Indies to accept your imports unless you accept her exports.
I think the time has come, Mr. Chairman when we might cut out this subsidy. 1 am sure that it would be of great assistance to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) if we did so.

My hon. friend (Mr. Garland) has stated that this country might well dispense with further subsidies to steamship services. That may be true as a general principle, but there are many cases in which it is quite proper and profitable for a country to subsidize a steamship service. At any rate, the reason my hon. friend gives for the abandonment of a subsidy to this service is not a sound one. He says the subsidies should not be further paid because we have a Canadian Merchant Marine. I say we should abandon our merchant marine and leave the carrying on of this service to private companies, even if we have to give them a subsidy; in the end it would be much cheaper for the country. I hope the Gov-
Steamship Services

eminent will very shortly make an effort to get rid of the steamships which they own and which they are operating at a very heavy loss-a loss which this country cannot very long sustain. I should like to point out further that many years ago a trade convention was negotiated between Canada and the British West Indies; I think it was some time between 1904 and 1908. Under that convention the West Indies received preferential treatment from Canada and we received preferential treatment in the West Indian markets. It was a part of that convention that we should establish a regular steamship service between Canada and the West Indies, suitable for the carrying of passengers and of the mails. I think the West India Islands contribute some small amount to the cost of this service. Now, the Canadian Merchant Marine are not capable of carrying out this service ac cording to the terms of that trade convention. The service between Canada and the West Indies has been a good thing for Canada and a good thing for the West Indies; therefore, I say we cannot look upon the matter as one involving merely the question of subsidy; it is tied up with the convention treaty with the West Indies. I suppose some steamship service would be carried on between Canada and the West Indies by private interests if there was no subsidized service, but it would not be a regular service. Our trade with the West Indies has been built up largely because of the fact that on a certain day every two weeks of the year a steamship sails from a Canadian port to the West Indies and on a certain day a steamship leaves a port in the West Indies for Canada. The Canadian exporters rely upon the regularity of the service, and the result is that Canadian trade has been very much built up. In that respect, therefore, there is some advantage in having (this subsidized service.
My hon. friend further stated that there had been a great diminution in export and import trade between the West Indies and Canada, and he compared the figures of last year with those of 1917-18. I have not studied the figures; I had not heard them until they were cited by my hon. friend. But I have no doubt that there were very good reasons for that decline in our trade with the West Indies when expressed in dollars. The products of the West Indies in 1917 were very high priced compared with those of to-day; Canadian products exported to the West Indies were very much

higher in price than they are to-day. A statement of the tonnage of this year as compared with that of 1917 would be a truer reflection of the volume of trade being carried on to-day as compared with that carried on in 1917. The decrease in the prices of commodities would explain a great deal of the difference between the figures for this year and those for 1917-18. It may be said also that the decline in this trade is owing partly to the world-wide depression which has prevailed.
I should like to say just a few words to the minister. I understand that this subsidized service between the Wes! Indies and Canada was renewed e few months ago for two years more Trade between Canada and the Wes' Indies has developed so much in recent years that the present four steamers engaged in that service are hardly sufficient to meet the trade requirements, and in other respects the boats used are not equal to the demands for passenger service. The contract is with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. They are quite willing to build four new steamers. They realize that the present boats are hardly fitted for the business to-day, but they do not feel warranted in proceeding with the construction of new boats unless they are sure that they are to have a contract covering a considerable period of time. It would take some time to complete the construction of two or three boats, and I think it is only fair that they should be advised as soon as possible whether or not the contract is to be renewed for a definite and extended period.
As I have said, I do not think that this service could be carried on without a subsidy. The people of the West Indies insist upon a passenger service, and that could not be carried on except by subsidized boats.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the Canadian Merchant Marine cannot come up to the requirements set out in the statute embodying the Canada-West Indies trade agreement?

No; they have no steamers suitable for carrying on the service. They are not fitted with passenger accommodation, and their deck construction is not fitted for the carrying on of trade in tropical countries. It is true that some of these steamers might be reconstructed to meet demands of that character.

Steamship Services

I am
afraid the hon. member is a little in error in this matter. Some of our merchant marine have already been equipped for passenger service.

A very
limited service indeed. They would not be equal to the passenger demands that are made on the subsidized boats.

There is
no reason why they should not be. They have been equipped for this very service to the West Indies. I would also submit to the minister that last year the then Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) stated-definitely, as appears on page 1488 of Hansard, that this subsidy was simply being continued for another year in order to give an opportunity of getting an improved weekly service. The department has had a whole year in which to think it over, and I now move, Mr. Chairman, that this item be struck out.

We are very glad indeed to hear the hon. member from Bow River discuss the service between Halifax and the West Indies. It seems to me that before moving to strike out this item, he should try and find out what he is talking about. In making his motion, he shows that he is entirely without knowledge of the facts concerning this service, and when he talks about the Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessels being able to carry on this service, he shows he knows absolutely nothing about the subject. Will my hon. friend believe me when I say that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessels can carry only eighteen passengers, while the Royal Mail steamers carry two hundred? During the winter months these subsidized boats are full to capacity with people from Montreal, Quebec, and other parts of Quebec, going south to winter in the Bahamas and other islands in the West Indies. Yet the hon. member from Bow River, three thousand miles from the coast, comes here and tells the committee that these boats are not required, and that the subsidy should be cut off.

I did not
say that the service was not required, but that the subsidy was unjustifiable, and I still maintain that.

What reason can you give
for cutting off the subsidy?

I have
given my reasons.

The hon. member has given no sound reason whatever. He knows nothing about it. This service cannot be carried on without a subsidy. It is a very important service to the people of Canada, and just as important to the people living in the hon. member's province as it is to people in the East because these boats carry flour, cereals and other products of Western Canada to the West Indies. These boats leave Halifax fortnightly for the West Indies carrying passengers and mails and Canadian products, and bring back from the West Indies good? which are required in Canada. If the subsidy is cut off, these boats will not be able to carry on the service, and therefore I would ask the hon. member to withdraw his motion.

The
amendment of the hon. member for Bow River, being simply negative, is out of order. His remedy, if he is opposed to the item, is to vote against it.

I should like to convince my hon. friend from Bow River that he should support the item as presented. It is quite true that the intimation was made that the contract was expiring and that new tenders were to be asked for, but the purpose in asking for new tenders was to provide an even better service, so as to carry out our obligations to the West Indies under the treaty that was made. As has already been intimated iby the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) Canadians go down to the West Indies in the winter season, and West Indies come up to Canada in the summer season, and i is just possible when my hon. friend goes home he may run across some West Indians who have come to the foothills of the Rockies to escape the heat of the southern clime.

I will
let the minister know if I find any.

For the information of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) the government in September last called for tenders, which were opened on the 31st of January. The only tender received was from the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, which asked for a net return of 71 per cent on the investment. That was more than the government would agree to, so to carry out our obligations to the people of the West Indies and continue the service, we have simply renewed the old agreement for a period of two years. In the mean-
Steamship Services

time we shall see what will develop. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre to-night has introduced another idea, which with other suggestions will be taken into consideration. I am sure that when the Minister of Railways takes up his estimates, he will satisfy the hon. member for Bow River that there are no vessels in the merchant marine equipped to carry out the promise we made to the West Indies when they gave us a preference in that market.
Has the minister reference to the treaty negotiated the year before last with the West Indies?
Yes.
It was just a renewal of the old treaty.

In reference to the item before us, this subsidy is given, I understand, in view of the treaty. Of course, this Government must carry out the obligations that have been entered into with the West Indies. The question whether the subsidy is justified or not might be debatable, but I think that the carrying out of our obligations under the treaty is an aspect of the question that my hon. friend from Bow River did not take into account when he moved to strike out the item. Those obligations must be lived up to.
As to the Government Merchant Marine, my own view is that those vessels should be used wherever they can be used to carry on the trade of this country, but they were not built as passenger vessels. The Government Merchant Marine was built as a freight marine, and consequently the vessels are not equipped for the particular trade between Canada and the West Indies at the present time. The people of Nova Scotia and of eastern Canada generally who are prosperous can afford to spend a few months in the West Indies in the winter.
I have met some Winnipegers down there too.

There may be also some from the remote West who can afford to go to the West Indies during our cold winter. I believe entirely in the development of trade with the West Indies and with the outside world wherever we can develop it. I hope to see that trade expand and grow. I might draw the attention of the committee to this fact, and I have mentioned it when this question was under consideration in preceding sessions, that it is rather inconsistent to subsidize 
steamships for the promotion of trade with other countries and at the same time maintain a system of tariffs that makes trade with those countries almost impossible. I think that when my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce gives this question that careful thought and study that he gives to problems that come before his deparment, he will realize the truth of what I say, and I am very hopeful that when another session comes round he will be among the ardent supporters in this House of a substantial reduction in the tariff.
This is the first time the matter has been drawn to my attention; I will look into it.

It causes me great regret to realize that owing to my remarks I have incurred the contumely of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). As a general rule his criticisms are directed at the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen).
That is a very smart observation on the part of the hon. gentleman.

I feel
very flattered to know that the remarks directed at me also apply to the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie), because the latter last year raised the same point that I have raised to-night. On that occasion the Solicitor General protested against the continuance of this subsidy. He stated his reasons very clearly and I have read them to the committee, but I suppose the hon. member for Lunenburg was not in the House at the time. With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) the agreement between this country and the Canadian government does not call for a subsidized steamship line, it calls for a steamship freight and passenger service. On the other hand it is declared that if a subsidized service is arranged for, then something else will berequired. Whatwill be required is that the governments of the colonies in question shall arrange for bungalows, hotels, and other accommodation for the class of passengers that are carried on these vessels. I am sorry that unfortunately conditions in the West will prevent me from going to the West Indies and taking advantage of this kind of accommodation.

Why not go to
California?

Nor shall I be able to go even to that land of sunshine; I must remain in Canada under present conditions of agriculture. I repeat that all that is asked for in the agreement referred to is that the government of Canada shall use its best endeavours to arrange for a passenger and freight service to go into effect as soon as possible. It is not necessary to have this service subsidized.

The vessels now subsidized by the Canadian government run from Halifax to the West Indies, and in return from the West Indies to St. John, and cater for freight and passengers. There is considerable freight, and also a very considerable number of passengers, carried by that line. I know this because the service comes under my observation regularly every year. The suggestion advanced by an hon. gentleman to my left is that this trade could be done by the vessels of the Government Merchant Marine. I would like to point out that those vessels were built for the carriage of freight not for the carriage of passengers. Now the accommodation for passengers on the service between the West Indies and St. John and Halifax must be suitable. It must also be comfortable; otherwise, it would not be used. I do not think it at all likely that the freight boats owned by the government could be made suitable for the comfort and convenience of passengers. I am therefore of the opinion that in this case the subsidies should be continued in order to provide a suitable and popular service between the West Indies and the ports of Halifax and St. John.

How is the amount of this subsidy determined? Was there any competition before the amount was arrived at? I think we ought to know at least that we are protected in the matter of the amount of this subsidy.
The contract was renewed at the same rate that had prevailed heretofore.
How do we know that the subsidy is not five times too large?
As a matter of fact the company demanded a higher rate. We advertised for tenders and their's was the lowest, indeed the only, tender that was received in public competition.
The contract was originally put up for tender?

Item agreed to.
Steamship Services
Canada and Australian or New Zealand, or both, on the Pacific ocean, steam service between, $130,509.

I notice that the imports from New Zealand have decreased very rapidly and are back to the figures of 1912. I would like to know if the minister has had this fact under his consideration in connection with the giving of this particular subsidy? As a matter of fact the imports into this country from New Zealand last year totalled only $783,500 as compared with something like over $7,000,000 worth at one time.

I think your figures axe incorrect. The figures appear to be-
1914	 $3,000,000
1920. .		 3,494,000
1921	 4,219,000
For the year ending 31st March, 1922, according to the figures furnished by the department, the amount was $1,000,000 odd.
Yes. Perhaps my hon. friend will agree with me that it may be more a shrinkage of value than of tonnage.
To whom were these subsidies paid for the Australian serivice?
They were paid to the Union Steamship Company of New Zealand, and the agents of this company are the Cana-dian-Australian Royal Mail Line.

How long was the contract for?
Mr. ROB'B: This contract expires on July 31st, 1922. The service is also subsidized by the postal authorities of England, who recently inquired if we would be willing to extend the contract until March 31st, 1924, so that our contract should run concurrently with theirs, and we agreed to that. This contract has been renewed until March 31st, 1924, and1 this service forms the only connection between Canada and New Zealand.

In respect to a great many of these subsidies, I think the Government would be well advised to take into consideration, if not the total abrogation, at any rate, a reduction, of some of them. I think there are cases where subsidies are justified, but it is a very easy matter, when you have developed the habit of giving subsidies, to continue giving them, whether the case merits it or not, and the services now between Australia, New Zealand and Canada are pretty well looked after by various

steamship lines. There is competition in the service, and when you get competition of an active kind in a service, surely the need for subsidies must disappear. That does not exist in the case of a subsidy we were considering to the West Indies a few moments ago, but, in the case where, practically one continent is trading with another continent, there should be sufficient competition, so that subsidies should not be necessary to maintain the necessary services, and I trust the 'Government will take that fact into their careful consideration, as these subsidies expire.

There is very much force in the argument of my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). Indeed this particular subsidy bas been decreased. It was $180,000 and it has been reduced to $130,-
000.	There is much farce in the argument that as trade develops they should be selfsustaining.
For how many years Will these contracts run as a rule? How long are we tied up by them?

Some of these contracts are given for a period of years. This particular one extends for two years, until March 31st, 1924, but in all these contracts there is a clause stating that it is subject to a vote by Parliament, so that, if Parliament to-night refuses to vote the amount, it Is cancelled.

Item agreed to.
Pelee Island and the mainland-steam service between, $11,000.
Where is Pelee Island?
On Lake Erie.

Item agreed to.
Quebec, Natashquan and Harrington, and Bras d'Or and other ports on the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, steam service between, $85,000.
There is an increase in that?

That provides for an increased service. It is a considerably better service. Last year there was one steamer employed in the service. The contractors this year have put on two vessels, the North Shore and the Labrador, with which they are performing a weekly service, running the North Shore every two weeks to Natashquan, calling at Anticosti Island, and running the Labrador every two weeks

Steamship Services
to Harrington and other way ports between Harrington and Bras d'Or hay. This extension of this service to Bras d'Or bay is expected to divert the trade of that part of the coast which in the past has been going to Newfoundland, to Canada, and in view of the fact that this increase has been given to the North Shore service, the contractors have, although it is not so specified in the contract, much improved their south shore service, having put on a large new steamer, the Gaspesia, of about 1,200 tons.
What is the real need for this subsidy, or is there any? It seems to me rather a remarkable thing that steamships running up and down the gulf of St. Lawrence should require a subsidy.

Yes, if there is one service in all the list that is needed, it is this service. It extends 626 miles east from Quebec city, down along the north shore of the St. Lawrence, where there is no railway. There are settlers established along there, and the service has developed industries along the coast.
It is the only communication they have with the outside world.

Will the minister do something to extend and improve the service between Murray Bay and Tadoussac? On the 11th April last year I introduced a resolution, urging upon the Government the establishment of a steamboat service between Murray Bay and Tadoussac, especially for the winter months, or from November to May. Last year, when the late government was in office, we were refused the service because it was claimed it was not necessary. This year I have presented to the Government petitions from all the boards of trade in the county, but, up to the present time, I have not received any favourable answer. I think the hon. minister might give me an answer.

It is only fair to say to my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) that he has bombarded my office, I would not say every day, but, at least, once a week, since the opening of the session, and knowing, as you all know, what a nice pleasant chap he is, you can understand how hard it is to resist his demands. We have subsidized a small service from St. Catharine's bay to Tadoussac for the winter season. That was passed some time ago. I understand he wants a somewhat wider service, but I think he will have to
exercise patience for, at least, this year. I will not commit myself to what will be done next year.

The people living between Muray Bay and Tadoussac have no good railway service, and no good roads, especially in the winter season; therefore, this steam service is very necessary for them and would serve a useful purpose.
We will take it under consideration.

Item agreed to.
St. John and Digby, steam service between, $15,000.
That is across the bay of Fundy?
Yes.
What is the explanation for the increase?

The subsidy in 1920-21 was $20,000. Then it was reduced to $10,000. The company has submitted a statement showing a very heavy operating loss amounting to nearly $100,000 in three years, and it states that unless the subsidy is increased the service will be discontinued. It is the only service these people have.

Item agreed to.
Sydney and Whycocomagh, steam service between, $7,000.
What are the particulars of this item?

This is one of the oldest services that we have subsidized. It was carried on by an old steamer, the Marion, and the directors have been endeavouring to secure a new boat. In consideration of a new and better steamer being put on the route we promised a subsidy of |$7,000, bult they have been unable so far to secure such a steamer. The Marion is being repaired, and in view of the expense involved in the work we have consented to pay them $5,000, and have also agreed that if they succeed in getting a better steamer we will pay them the $7,000.

Item agreed to.
RAILWAY® AND CANALS
Railways and Canals-Loan to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, $4,360,720.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. C. KENNEDY (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
The amount required for payment of bank advances,



Supply-Merchant Marine
outstanding vouchers, and insurance premiums, payable as at the 31st December, 1921, was $3,000,000. The estimated amount required to meet deficit in operations, on the basis of operating thirty-seven vessels for the year ending 31st December, 1922, is $1,000,000, and to carry on to the end of the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1923, there is an additional estimate for the three months of $250,000, making a total of $1,250,000. The amount required for capital expenditure on the vessels is $110,720, making a total in all, as outlined in the estimates, of $4,360,720.
What is the nature of the capital expenditure of $110,000 odd?
I will read the particulars.
Is the amount properly chargeable to capital?

Yes, these
items are: Two propellers at $5,500 each, $11,000; superheater, $11,500; steam driers, 20 at $150 each, $3,000; soot blowers, 20 at $1,366, $27,320; governors, 20 at $1,100, $22,000; intakes 4 at $600, $2,400; winches, 14 at $1,100, $15,400;-
That is quite enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

Before you write that "carried", Mr. Chairman, I want to ask another question. . I do not recall any statement of the operations of the merchant marine having been submitted this session. Will such a statement be included in the annual report of the Canadian National Railways, which I understand has been published?

The report
of the Canadian National Railways will be tabled in a day or two and, incorporated in it, a statement in regard to the merchant marine for the past year.

A statement showing
profit and loss in operation?

Yes, and
giving the report of the directors.

I think we ought to
have some information in connection with the merchant marine.

I shall be
glad to give my hon. friend any information he requires to-night.

I would like to know what you are going to do with the mer-
:Mr. W. C. Kennedy.)
chant marine? You have sixty-five boats and those of less than 5,000 tons, I think, will never pay. I do not think they will pay operating expenses. These boats are deteriorating in value all the time. I do not think they should be kept by the Government.
There is no doubt about that.

I may tell
the hon. member that his views coincide with those of the board of directors of the National Railways. There are twenty-seven smaller vessels which they propose to lay up this year twenty of which are in fact laid up at the present time. It is the intention to dispose of them to the best possible advantage, retaining the larger ones for the time being. This matter, as in the past, will be dealt with by the board of directors.

The construction of these ships has been criticised by some people, but it was a policy initiated during the war, and might very well be looked upon as an insurance premium against national loss. The construction of the ships was undertaken at a time when it looked as though the German submarine warfare would be most disastrous to British shipping the world over. It was the desire of the British government as well that Canada should at that time construct ships, and the policy was supported by every member in Parliament as well as by the Canadian people at large. The policy had reference only to the construction of ships to bridge us over the imminent danger that existed at that time. It was never the settled policy of the government that they should] continue the ownership and operation of these vessels, and I think that the Government should divest itself of that ownership. The vessels are being operated at a tremendous loss, and it is the experience and the judgment of those men who are best able to speak on such matters that government operation of ships must inevitably be carried on at a loss. The United States constructed about 1,500 ships for the same reasons that we built 60 or 70. About 1,000 of those ships are now laid up in the ports of the United States. The others are being operated at a net annual loss of $50,000,000. The policy of the United States is to get rid of these ships just as soon as they can, but they find it rather difficult to do so. The head of the United States Shipping Board, in an address delivered lately at Washington, stated that in his judgment it was not

Supply-Merchant Marine
sound public policy for the people of the United States to further continue the operation of these ships by the government.
Now, I submit that it is not fair for us to have government-operated ships in competition with shipping services originated, developed and carried on by private companies which have devoted much time and money to the building up of their business. They find themselves in the position of facing the competition of government-owned boats operating at a loss, which loss they, the owners of these privately operated ships, have to help pay.
Last year I called attention to the fact that there were two or three steamship lines operating between Canada and Newfoundland, none of which are subsidized. These services were started many years ago and there is a great deal of Canadian money invested in them. The Canadian Merchant Marine saw fit to enter into competition with these long-established services when those services were quite capable of handling all the business that was offering. The result is that these privately owned services are being slowly destroyed, they cannot stand this one-sided competition much longer, and ultimately they will have to go out of business altogether. In a year or so our government-owned boats will be worn out, and we certainly will never embark on a construction policy again. Consequently we will have no service at all between our ports and Newfoundland, and the time, energy and money put into the development of these privately-established services will be absolutely lost and we shall not have gained anything in return. If we ever hope to establish a merchant marine our only chance is in encouraging private capital to embark in the enterprise.
Now, what should be done with our government-owned ships? I would suggest to the Minister of Railways that he immediately take into consideration the advisability of parting ownership with them. I would advise him to endeavour to sell the ships to Canadians so they may be under Canadian registry if possible. If proposing purchasers have not the money to pay down, I would advise him to take a mortgage for the full amount of the purchase price, asking the purchasers, of course, to insure the ships up to the amount of the mortgage. I think it would be preferable to get rid of these ships rather than operate them through government agencies. In the event of his not being able
to sell them, I would suggest that he turn over their operation to Canadian shipping companies. It is not sound business to be operating these ships at a loss of $10,000,000 a year. And they never will pay their way. It is the one class of business that a government is absolutely unfitted to engage in. You can make an argument in favour of government ownership and operation of railways, because the railway business is in the nature of a monopoly, but in shipping free trade exists, and there is more than enough tonnage to-day to do the world's shipping business. Our shipping needs can be amply met if we dispense with our government-owned boats and depend on the service which the shipping of the world to-day affords.
I cannot conceive of any sound reason justifying further continuance of the operation of these ships by the Government. I am not entering any complaint against the management. I have no doubt they are doing the best they can and are zealous in the development of the service; but unfortunately there is the result, and it always will be that way. If there was any national interest being served by continuing our ownership and operation I might submit to the policy, I suppose, but in the circumstances I cannot see any justification whatever for such continuation, and I hope if the Minister of Railways has not already power to dispose of these ships, that he take steps before the session ends to secure the necessary enabling powers to deal with any possible situation that may develop in connection with their disposal.

With a great deal of what my hon. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has said, I agree. He has stated the reasons, whether they were good reasons or not at the time, that led to the building of this merchant marine. Unquestionably the country cannot go on facing the heavy losses that result in the operation of these ships. A suggestion has been made by one of my hon. friends from British Columbia that the smaller vessels will prove of no value and should be disposed of. My hon. friend from Halifax would go further and dispose of the whole lot. It occurs to me that the larger vesesls might be of some use as complementary to the railway system which the country has. I do not know how far that would be justified on sound, business principles, but I do know that other transportation companies have water connection in ocean-going vessels, and I would suggest
Supply-Merchant Marine

to the minister not to display the eager haste which my hon. friend from Halifax counselled in disposing of these vessels, particularly the larger ones. I think the question of their disposition should be thoroughly inquired into.

If my hon. friend will allow me to interrupt a moment -I did intend to qualify my remarks somewhat in the direction indicated by him. It might be desirable, particularly if it be found difficult to dispose of the larger ships, to continue their operation in the ocean services. There is something to he said for that.

That is what I had in mind. The whole situation should be carefully canvassed and examined before these vessels are disposed of at bargain-counter prices or given away to the first person who will take them. The smaller vessels will not be of service in that respect. I do not know whether it would be possible to make use of them on the lakes where smaller boats can be Used, but at any rate I agree with my hon. friend that this is a question which should receive the attention of the board of directors of the National Railways.
There is one other thought that I have to offer in that connection. Even if disposition of these vessels is made by sale, I do not know that the present time is best suited for the purpose. We know that trade has been depressed in the last few years greater than it has ever been in the memory of any within reach of my voice tonight. We believe that trade conditions are going to revive, and that in a few years' time the commercial world will be resuming operations on something like the old scale. Unquestionably at that time a greater demand for ships will arise. My suggestion to the minister would be not to act too hastily in this connection; it is possible that a year or two hence he would get a much better price for the vessels, or for those that the board of directors of the National Railways wished to sell, than could possibly be got at the present time.

Every country has to have a merchant marine in connection with the solution of its transportation problems. This matter was partly discussed in the debate on the naval estimates; the value of a merchant marine, not only for ordinary purposes of trade and commerce but in time of war, was brought out. One of the reasons why England is the great commercial country that she is to-day and has been for

centuries is found in the operations of her merchant marine. Drake, Frobisher, Hawkins-all these men were men of the merchant marine; their activities were the foundation of the great trade and commerce of the Mother Country. Australia and New Zealand have taken a leaf out of the Mother Country's book. The Government have said that they are going to give the National Railways a chance. What kind of chance is it going to be? If some of the papers in the Montreal district had their way, the National Railways would be under the control of the Canadian Pacific, and so would Canada's merchant marine; and it would be a sorry day for Canada if that took place. Look at what the United States are doing in an effort to solve their transportation problems; they have turned all their war plants into peace plants. Government ships as well as ships for private concerns are being built with a view to holding the great trade that came to the United States as a result of the war. Canada also took a leading part in the war; is she to dispose of her merchant marine, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) ? It is true that these ships were built rather from the unemployment standpoint than from the economic standpoint; they cost a great deal more than the price at which they could have been purchased in the old land. But if we are to make a success of our National Railways we must provide feeders for them -ocean feeders as well as lake feeders. It is true that there have been deficits1, and we may expect them for some time to come. But take a case of private ownership: the Canadian Pacific did not pay when it was first started; not until ocean services, lake services and hotel services were added to the rail system was success achieved. I say that if we are to fulfil the important part we should play in the Empire in the future we must go out on the seven seas and secure our share of the world's trade. The people of the United States have had deficits in connection with their merchant marine. The same criticisms were offered in Australia but both in that country and in New Zealand the operations were extended and large surpluses were subsequently obtained. I am surprised, Mr. Chairman, at the carping criticism which has been offered in respect to this item. The minister has been doing the best he could; he has made very substantial progress and I think the committee should give the merchant marine a chance. If they

Supply-Merchant Marine
will not do that, then we may as well cut off the railways as well, because the two are interlocked. It has been established by evidence submitted to the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States and by reports made to Congress and to the Senate at Washington that steam roads cannot operate profitably without feeders in the way of ocean and lake services. In my opinion this is a vote in the right direction; instead of being curtailed it ought to be increased. If these various services are operated on business lines there is no doubt in my mind that within a few years we shall have in them a great asset.
Are any of the ships of the Canadian Merchant Marine engaged in carrying Canadian wheat and flour to the British market?
I am not in a position to give an answer at the moment, but I am inclined to think they are not at present; they are not suitable for it.
Is this the last railway item?
Yes.
May I be permitted to put a question to the minister under this head with regard to a railway matter?
Yes:

I would inquire whether the Government have had any proposal from the government of New Brunswick with reference to what is known as the Valley Railway? From answers to questions put some time ago in the House it appears that in the taking over of the Canadian Northern, Ontario was in effect relieved of obligations amounting to over $7,000,000; Manitoba of over $25,000,000; Saskatchewan, in connection with the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, of over $28,000,000; Alberta, in connection with the same lines, of about $21,000,000; British Columbia of about $40,000,000. These obligations are being met by the federal government. The St. John
Valley Railway was built for the purpose of connecting the Transcontinental _ with the port of St. John. It was not completed according to the original design, owing to the intervention of the war and to largely increased costs. But I notice that with some reductions which have been made it stands on the books of the province at something less than $7,000,000. It has cost the province $340,000 by way of interest, and it has also occasioned some loss to the federal government as well. It would seem to me that in fairness this road, which was constructed, as I say for the purpose of connecting the Transcontinental with the port of St. John, should be assumed by the federal government. It means the addition of a very considerable burden in proportion to the roads the liability for which has been removed from the other provinces. In fact, I think every province except Quebec and Prince Edward Island has shared in relief, and I trust the province of New Brunswick will not go without some measure of relief.

Now I do not wish to be misunderstood in what I have suggested. I did not suggest that the Government dispose of the larger vessels of 10,000 tons and up. I see no reason why they cannot be made profitable to this country, but the smaller vessels will never be an asset to Canada, and I think the Government should dispose of them.

There has,
so far as I know, been no definite proposal from the government of New Brunswick with respect to the sale of the railway to which my hon. friend from St. John refers. I did have an interview with two of the ministers, and that suggestion was made. The matter is now under consideration, but the Government is not in a position to say anything definite at the present time.
